progressItems.targetText: By 2030, reduce biodiversity loss and maintain ecological integrity by including all territory in spatial planning and ensuring effective management.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: Biodiversity conservation is no longer limited only to protected areas or focused solely on the conservation of endangered and rare species. Target 1 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) explicitly states that implementing planning across all territories and including all species increases the effectiveness of nature conservation. This target is a significant contribution to the implementation of Article 8 on "in-situ" conservation of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) . Mongolia also joined the Convention on Wetlands of International Importance (Ramsar) in 1998, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) in 1996, and the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) in 1999. In 2024, the State Great Khural approved the Regional Development Concept of Mongolia, which defines as one of its objectives the preservation of natural landscapes and ecosystem balance for future generations. With the approval of the National Programme on Soil Protection and Reduction of Land Degradation in 2019, a policy foundation was established to protect ecosystem integrity and promote sustainable use in agricultural regions. Resolution to Order No. 312 of the Minister of Environment dated 28 October 2009, work on conducting regional ecosystem assessments of Mongolia’s steppe ecosystems was initiated. As a result, the Ecological Regional Assessment was successfully carried out nationwide between 2011 and 2017. This has enabled ecosystem-level inventory and created opportunities to integrate ecosystem considerations into development planning. A major achievement in ensuring the reduction of biodiversity loss and the conservation of ecological integrity through comprehensive spatial planning is the approval by the General Authority for Land Administration, Geodesy and Cartography of the Methodology for the General Land-Use Plan of Aimag and Capital City and the Methodology for Soum Territorial Development Planning . These two methodologies explicitly include provisions to: (2.1.12) address climate change impacts, risks, vulnerabilities, and adaptation measures; (2.1.13) promote sustainable use that incorporates biodiversity conservation and the maintenance of ecosystem naturalness; and (2.1.17) protect the characteristics of natural zones and belts, unique formations, areas containing rare and endangered flora and fauna, as well as historical, cultural, and scenic sites. These provisions constitute key measures for achieving National Target 1. Furthermore, the BIOSAN software, which has been used and developed since 2009, has been upgraded into the BIOSAN – Wildlife and Plant Monitoring Database , establishing a foundational information system to identify the distribution, location, and abundance of plant and animal species. In addition, databases related to species distribution, key habitats, ecological corridors, and breeding areas have been developed and integrated into the EGAZAR 2.0 platform , and are now operational. Beyond these initiatives, the Computerized Mining Cadastre System , administered by the Authority for Mineral Resources and Petroleum, has become a core system for registering areas under local protection.

progressItems.progressSummary: To reduce biodiversity loss and maintain ecological integrity, Mongolia continues efforts to integrate all land areas into spatial planning and ensure effective management. As a priority, data and information related to internationally significant rare and endangered species of flora and fauna, ecosystems, water resources, and wetlands are being systematically consolidated and incorporated into relevant national and international databases. Within the framework of Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs), a total of 69 sites covering 9,908,605 hectares have been identified and registered in Mongolia. Of these, 25 sites covering 7,686,384 hectares are located within nationally designated protected areas. In addition, 70 Important Bird Areas (IBAs) covering 7,906,557 hectares have been identified (), of which 69 sites have been assessed under Criterion A1. In 2025, Mongolia prepared and submitted its National Report under the Ramsar Convention. A total of 11 wetland sites, covering 1,439,530 hectares, were designated as wetlands of international importance for water resources, wetlands, and waterbirds. Of the 11 wetlands listed under the Ramsar List, 8 sites are located within nationally designated protected areas.  During 2026–2027, Mongolia is working to nominate Lake Khövsgöl and the Tengis, Shishkhed Depression for designation under the Ramsar Convention . Significant work has been carried out under the land cover classification framework, and this report reflects the ecosystem classification developed by UNEP-WCMC. According to this classification, Mongolia’s land area is composed of bare land with sparse vegetation (42.46%), desert (22.66%), steppe (20.14%), agricultural land (6.48%), forest (4.92%), shrub steppe (2.07%), rivers and lakes (0.94%), wetlands (0.24%), urban and settlement areas (0.05%), and permanent snow and ice (0.04%).
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: For Target 1, key challenges include insufficient cross-sectoral policy coherence—particularly in aligning livestock, agriculture and mining with biodiversity objectives—along with the need to clearly assign stakeholder roles and responsibilities under the National Biodiversity Programme and establish a robust monitoring and evaluation (M&E) system. Monitoring, accountability and incentive mechanisms also remain weak for effectively engaging government, NGOs, citizens and the private sector. Further implementation should strengthen inter-sectoral coordination, link public and private budgets/financing to Target 1 actions, ensure institutional stability, and improve M&E and accountability systems (including incentives) at all levels. Mongolia reports continued progress toward Target 1 by shifting from a protected-area-only approach to biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning and effective management across all territories. Key outcomes include: (i) strengthened national policy direction to safeguard ecosystem integrity in development planning; (ii) completion of a nationwide ecological regional assessment (2011–2017) that improved ecosystem inventories for planning; (iii) adoption of official aimag/capital and soum territorial planning methodologies that require biodiversity considerations (e.g., maintaining ecosystem naturalness, protecting habitats of rare and endangered species and other sensitive areas, and integrating climate risk); and (iv) improved national biodiversity data and monitoring systems (including an upgraded wildlife and plant monitoring database and the integration of species distribution, key habitats, ecological corridors and breeding areas into national spatial information systems), supporting more evidence-based land-use decisions. In addition, challenges have emerged due to limited capacity to systematically integrate information and research outputs from international organizations into national systems. These include: (i) inconsistencies in land-cover classification and weak interoperability across registration and information systems; (ii) fragmented biodiversity, ecosystem and protected-area datasets across multiple platforms, which require better integration and more flexible, user-friendly access; (iii) insufficient efforts to clearly delineate and register boundaries for locally protected areas, biodiversity-important areas, Important Bird Areas, and Ramsar-listed lakes and wetlands in existing databases; (iv) inadequate research on the distribution, abundance, key habitats, ecological corridors and breeding areas of plant and animal species; and (v) the growing need to implement the Ecosystem Red List Assessment (a key national indicator) by consolidating existing information and applying international best practices to generate the required data in the coming years.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: With the introduction of the Methodology for the General Land-Use Plan of Aimag and Capital City and the Methodology for Soum Territorial Development Planning, it has become possible to conserve, monitor, and assess ecosystem integrity, as well as the distribution, abundance, and habitats of flora and fauna. In particular, the General Authority for Land Administration, Geodesy and Cartography has developed and manages the platform Egazar , within which a dedicated sub-database titled “Biodiversity Statistics” has been established. This database currently records and spatially visualizes species distribution ranges, key habitats, ecological corridors, breeding areas, and mating grounds for wildlife. At present, the distribution ranges of 145 animal species are displayed based on International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) distribution data. In addition, key habitats and ecological corridors for six priority species —the Mongolian saiga, goitered gazelle, Mongolian gazelle, Gobi bear, khulan, and snow leopard—have been identified and mapped separately. In addition, a research report initiated by DBHS on the distribution and ecological corridors of rare and migratory wildlife in Mongolia has been produced. This study is expected to make a significant contribution to the further enrichment and updating of the above-mentioned databases in 2026. According to IUCN data (2022), 17% of the world's land and 8% of the oceans are under protection; Mongolia's land protection level is above the global average. However, there is a need to balance diverse ecosystems and representative natural features. Studies show that 13.7% of high-mountain ecosystems, 6.0% of forest-steppes, 6.0% of steppes, 23.5% of desert ecosystems, and approximately 40% of the distribution areas of endangered species are covered by state special protection. Conversely, steppe and peatland ecosystems have very low coverage, and river headwaters and certain forest zones remain outside protection boundaries. National land-use planning made more transparent and actionable ( EGAZAR platform ): Mongolia operationalized an online land-use planning system where approved plans can be viewed at national/aimag/soum levels and draft plans can receive public input—supporting whole-of-territory planning and accountability. Biodiversity monitoring mainstreamed into government practice ( BIOSAN → national system ): The protected and conserved area biodiversity monitoring database BIOSAN was upgraded and officially handed over to the responsible ministry, strengthening standardized field monitoring and data use for management decisions.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, restore at least 30 percent of degraded ecosystems and improve ecological integrity and connectivity.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: Mongolia is focusing on the restoration of degraded ecosystems by implementing land protection and reclamation activities. In 2024, a total of 3,673,616.02 hectares nationwide were covered by land protection and restoration measures; however, this represents a decrease of 222,138.14 hectares compared to the previous year. A detailed breakdown of the 2024 restored areas is as follows: Pastureland: 3,141,337.8 hectares Forest area: 246,253.77 hectares Agricultural land: 175,032.10 hectares Water area: 56,517.78 hectares Urban settlements: 26,884.17 hectares State Special Purpose land: 22,567.01 hectares Mining land reclamation: 1,790.5 hectares Roads and infrastructure networks: 67.89 hectares In 2024, out of the total 175,032.10 hectares of agricultural land where protection and restoration measures were implemented, 108 hectares specifically involved the restoration of severely eroded farmland and abandoned (fallow) lands. Additionally, protection and restoration efforts were applied to 3,141,337.8 hectares of pastureland in 2024. This accounts for 85.5% of the total land area covered by such measures nationwide and represents an increase of 398,798.49 hectares compared to the previous year. Since the majority of Mongolia's degraded ecosystems consist of pasturelands, a nationwide network of research and monitoring plots was established in 2015 to assess rangeland status. As of 2025, this network has expanded to 5,333 monitoring points . To support this, several provincial and soum-level Citizens' Representative Commitees have formally adopted and enforced “ Regulations on Accountable Pastureland Use ”. According to 2021 data, the implementation of sustainable management practices through the photomonitoring program resulted in the recovery of 20.6 million hectares of healthy pastureland . Furthermore, under the ENSURE project (2019–2025), five-year rangeland management plans were implemented in the Gobi region. As a result, 23.4% of participating herders reduced their livestock numbers, successfully lowering the grazing pressure on the land . Within the framework of mining concession protection and reclamation, the following activities were completed in 2024: 2,165.26 hectares of excavated and degraded land were backfilled and leveled, 1,769.48 hectares underwent biological reclamation (revegetation), and 1,020.64 hectares of riverbanks were restored and their natural flows reinstated. Regarding urban settlements and villages, protection and restoration efforts in 2024 included: 25,919.19 hectares planted with trees and shrubs, and 28.65 hectares of topsoil restoration and landscaping (lawns). Under the initiative of the President of Mongolia, U. Khurelsukh, the "One Billion Trees" national movement was launched in 2021. The program is being successfully implemented, with 84 million trees planted as of 2024. These reforestation and forest restoration efforts are strategically directed toward several key environmental goals: Agricultural Land Restoration: Protecting and reclaiming farmland from degradation. Water Resource Protection: Conserving river basins, riparian zones, and water sources. Mining Reclamation: Restoring land affected by mining activities. Forest Restoration: Rehabilitating degraded forests and expanding forested areas. Urban Greening: Increasing green spaces within cities and settlements. To enhance reforestation and afforestation efforts and prevent forest degradation, the "Regulations on Forest Treatment and Cleaning" were updated and approved in 2020. Additionally, the cost norms for afforestation and forestry activities were revised in 2021. Figure 1. Map of the Forest distribution in Mongolia (2024) [1] [1] Forest resource of Mongolia. National Forest Agency, 2024. In the field of peatland protection and restoration, international researchers launched a five-year project in 2024, with plans to restore 20,000 hectares of peatlands. Figure 2. Map of peatland distribution in Mongolia [2] [2] Highland Peatlands of Mongolia, Tatiana Minayeva, Andrey Sirin, Chultemiin Dugarjav. 2024. Within the framework of restoring dried up and depleted lakes and ponds, several lake restoration projects have been implemented. For instance, in the territory of Delgerkhaan soum, Khentii aimag, the water volume of the Avarga Toson Lake—which is of exceptional medicinal significance—had decreased by 60% as of 2022 compared to 1970 levels [1] . Consequently, restoration work was carried out, and measures to protect and restore the lake and its surrounding shores were implemented [2] . Additionally, between 2021 and 2023, the project "Mitigating Desertification in the Darkhad Depression and Restoring Tsoitson Lake in Renchinlkhumbe Soum" was successfully implemented. Starting in 2021, a 403-meter dam was constructed on the Khodon River using engineering solutions, and a flow-diversion channel was excavated. As a result, the Khodon River began flowing 10.6 km along its original course to feed Tsoitson Lake, which was fully restored by 2023. Consequently, Tsoitson Lake is now capable of storing 35 million cubic meters of water [3] . Figure 3. progressItems.progressSummary: The Government of Mongolia is actively planning to restore no less than 30% of degraded ecosystems by 2030. As of 2024, 97.3% of the total damaged area consists of pastureland, highlighting an urgent need to accelerate rangeland restoration efforts. Currently, pastureland accounts for 85% of all areas where protection and restoration measures have been implemented. Additionally, the country aims to increase forest cover to 9% of the total land area by 2030. Since the current forest cover has reached 8.4% as of 2024, this objective is considered on track. However, intensive efforts are required between 2026 and 2030 to ambitiously implement the strategic plan to plant 1.5 billion trees, with a primary focus on the restoration of degraded ecosystems. According to data from 2023–2024, land protection and restoration measures are being implemented on 3.6 to 3.8 million hectares annually across the country. To meet Mongolia’s established targets, it is necessary to restore at least 30% of all degraded ecosystems by 2030. Achieving this requires the immediate identification and monitoring of degraded ecosystems as a baseline. Based on this monitoring, the annual target area for protection and restoration must be recalculated and expanded. The primary challenges to realizing these goals are insufficient enforcement of laws and regulations and financial constraints. For instance, there is a critical need to more effectively implement legal provisions that mandate reinvesting revenue from natural resource use fees back into environmental restoration.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Implementing the restoration and protection of degraded ecosystems through public participation, capacity building, and collaboration is considered critical to achieving these targets. However, increasing public engagement and enhancing the accountability of enterprises, citizens, and producers in restoration work remains a significant challenge. To address this, initiatives such as "Responsible Mining" and "Accountable Pastureland Use" are being implemented; however, there is an urgent need to transition toward participatory management methods. For instance, pasture management based on the regeneration capacity of vegetation must be implemented with the active assistance and participation of herders. According to 2024 data, the water levels of Mongolia's lakes and ponds have fluctuated significantly, with an increasing number of water bodies drying up. The primary drivers of this trend are climate change and shifts in precipitation patterns and frequency. Furthermore, the sustainable use of water resources is being hindered by inadequate planning regarding the number of water points, resource management, and rational utilization. Therefore, it is essential to integrate the restoration of rivers, streams, and lakes with efforts to expand surface water storage and implement flood regulation measures. As of 2024, the forest cover in Mongolia has reached 8.4% of the total land area. Within the framework of the "One Billion Trees" national movement, the target has been set at 1.5 billion trees—of which 667.2 million are specifically intended to expand forested areas. While 84 million trees have been planted as of 2024, the movement's strategy aimed to reach 240 million trees by 2025. This indicates a lag in implementation, highlighting the urgent need to improve performance. To address this, the initial phase requires strengthening tree nurseries and adopting advanced silvicultural technologies. Significant progress has been made in nursery capacity, growing from 32 million seedlings in 2010 to a reserve of 63 million in 2024. However, to meet long-term goals, both the quantity and quality of these seedlings must be further enhanced. Furthermore, human resource shortages are significantly impacting the broad-scale execution of forest regeneration, restoration, and afforestation efforts. To resolve this, universities have introduced part-time and evening programs for those interested in specializing in forestry, and additional classes have been added to Technical and Vocational Education Trainings (TVETs). Finally, to expand community-based tree planting, it is vital to increase public campaigns, provide professional advisory services, and support households in establishing green spaces. While there are currently two national tree-planting days, these should be expanded through localized campaigns to increase regional participation. The lack of consistent implementation and the premature repeal of environmental regulations, strategies, and policy documents have created an unstable legal environment, hindering progress toward national targets. Therefore, it is essential to guarantee the long-term sustainability and continuity of legal frameworks to ensure they remain in effect for their intended duration. At present, there is no official integrated baseline estimate for the total area of degraded ecosystems categorized by ecosystem type in Mongolia,. Furthermore, as land protection and restoration measures are recorded collectively, it is not possible to isolate the 'net restored' area from the total 3,673,616.02 hectares reported in 2024. Nevertheless, the implementation of restoration measures—such as mining reclamation, reforestation, sustainable pasture management, and wetland restoration—indicates that progress toward the target has commenced. Therefore, while there is evident progress, it can be concluded that the baseline data remains insufficient to quantitatively assess the specific percentage of target achievement. Main challenges: Lack of an integrated baseline inventory for degraded ecosystems. Lack of differentiation between land protection and restoration measures in national statistical records. Inconsistent measurement of ecosystem quality indicators (e.g., survival rates of seedlings, vegetation cover, and ecological integrity indices). Further: In 2026–2027, it is advisable to develop a classified national-level baseline map and assessment of degraded ecosystems and to record restoration and protection measures as separate categories within statistical classifications. In establishing national quality indicators to measure restoration outcomes, it is essential to incorporate pasture vegetation cover percentage (%), the 3-year survival rate of planted trees (%), and biodiversity stability assessments.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: Through the introduction of sustainable practices based on rangeland regeneration capacity and the implementation of measures to enhance accountability in livestock production, 20.6 million hectares of degraded pastureland have been restored nationwide over the past five years. This demonstrates the vital importance of collaborating with herders and pasture users to promote sustainable utilization of pastureland. In addition to forestry activities aimed at increasing forest cover, numerous initiatives outlined in the "One Billion Trees" national movement strategy are being implemented. Within this framework, spring and autumn tree-planting events are organized, reforestation and forest restoration works are conducted, and efforts to develop agro-forestry and expand urban green spaces are underway. These initiatives are increasing multi-stakeholder participation and improving ecological education among citizens. A key example of this progress is the "One Billion Trees Fund" initiated by banking and financial institutions, which has supported projects to expand green spaces and forested areas (selecting projects annually since 2022). In 2023 alone, 34 projects were implemented with 1.3 billion MNT in non-reimbursable financing, providing ecological education to 800,000 people, establishing over 20,000 square meters of green space, planting 105,000 trees, and completing reforestation and forest restoration on 37 hectares. The main cause of forest cover loss is forest insect pests and diseases. Consequently, in 2022, the "Technical Regulations for Combating Forest Pests and Diseases" were approved, leading to active prevention and control measures. In 2024, pest control operations were carried out across 243,000 hectares using state funding, with 100,000 hectares treated by aircraft and 143,000 hectares managed via backpack sprayers and mechanical methods. The volume of timber harvested from forests reached 696,400 cubic meters in 2023, a decrease of 27.1% compared to 2020. This decline reflects insufficient sustainable forest management activities and an unstable value-added chain for forest products, which in turn hinders the sustainable development of the forestry sector. progressItems.targetText: By 2030, 30% of the country's total area will be included in the special protected area network, representing major ecosystem types and strengthening ecological connectivity.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: On track to achieve target
reportedActions: In 1992, at the international conference initiated and organized by the UN and the World Wide Fund for Nature in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, a proposal was put forward to make our country a unique global biosphere region. In his speech at this conference, the first President of Mongolia, P. Ochirbat, expressed and declared to the world that he would take 30% of his country's total territory, or 46.9 million hectares, under special protection. By ratifying the "Convention on Biological Diversity" in 1993, the State Great Khural of Mongolia officially made Mongolia the 30th country in the world to join the convention. Subsequently, in 1994, the State Great Khural ratified the " Law on Special Protected Areas " establishing the legal environment for protected areas. In 1997, the Law on Buffer Zones of Special Protected Areas was approved, which became an important basis for organizing activities in the buffer zones of protected areas. Since its initial approval in 1994, the Law on Special Protected Areas has undergone a total of 17 amendments up until 2023, aimed at supporting international treaties and conventions joined by Mongolia and regulating legal relations arising from the development requirements of protected areas. In the "National Program on Special Protected Areas" (1998, updated in 2015, 2019, and 2021), a target was set to establish protection over at least 30% of the total territory. To bring 30% of the total land area under protection by 2030, it is necessary to include an additional 13.9–14.2 million hectares during the remaining period. In the Government of Mongolia's Action Plan for 2024–2028 , activities have been approved and are being implemented with the plan to take 43.8 million hectares, or 27.5% of the total territory, under state special protection by 2028. Currently, 20.8% of Mongolia's total territory, amounting to 31.3 million hectares, has been taken under special protection . There are a total of 120 state special protected areas in 102 locations, consisting of 22 strictly protected areas, 37 national parks, 47 nature reserves, and 14 natural monuments. Currently, 60% of these Special Protected Areas are in an isolated state without ecological connectivity between them. ‘Ecological connectivity’ refers to the possibility for any species and the natural processes that sustain living beings on Earth to move or migrate between each other without obstacles ( CMS, 2020 ). Without ecological connectivity areas, ecosystems cannot function normally, and without healthy ecosystems, biodiversity and other fundamental bases of life are put at risk. The disappearance or severance of ecological connectivity areas leads to human-induced ‘habitat fragmentation,’ which divides ecosystems and habitats into small, isolated pieces. In 2017–2020, in connection with the expansion of the special protected area network, the number of protection administrations grew to 33, the number of specialists to 127, and the number of rangers to 390. In 2024 alone, 41 billion MNT was spent from the state budget on the activities of state special protected area administrations. Due to the further expansion of the protected area network, these costs will continue to rise. In addition to the state budget, international projects and programs occupy a major position in the operations of protected area administrations. Through the German Credit Institute for Reconstruction (KfW), a project worth 15.3 million euros is being implemented with the goal of strengthening the management of special protected areas, focusing on improving the material base of protection administrations. To protect the biodiversity, unique ecosystems, and cultural heritage of the Onon-Balj National Park, the LLF is contributing within the framework of the "Eternal Mongolia" Project Finance for Permanence (PFP) program, with a project cost of approximately 15 million USD. The "Eternal Mongolia" program is a 198 million USD deal with a 15-year term for sustainable conservation financing; currently, 71 million USD has been centralized in the " Mongolia Nature's Heritage " conservation trust fund, which will be a major impetus for the conservation activities of special protected areas.

progressItems.progressSummary: In order to reach the national target, the legal and regulatory framework regarding Special Protected Areas (SPAs) was first defined. 1. The Law on Special Protected Areas was approved on November 15, 1994, and has been followed since April 1, 1995. Since its approval, a total of 17 amendments have been made. 2. The Law on Buffer Zones of Special Protected Areas was approved on October 23, 1997, and 2 amendments have been made to the law. Article 3, Section 2 of the Law on Special Protected Areas states: "Aimags, the capital city, soums, and districts may take certain areas within their territories under local special protection." As of September 1, 2020, 2,678 locations of aimags and the capital city, or 42.26 percent of the total territory, have been taken under local special protection. Taking land under special protection is creating several challenges for Mongolia. First of all, 30% of the total territory is a very large area in itself. Financial and human resource challenges in conducting conservation activities in these areas are increasingly growing. It is necessary to resolve the size of the area managed by a single ranger relative to established standards, as well as the equipment related to implementing conservation activities and the financing of their operational costs. In reality, judging from evaluations made on the fact that a single ranger is responsible for an area "several times" larger than the established standard, the necessity for increased conservation and other related costs as new state special protected areas are added, and the experiences of other countries, there is an urgent need to increase the types of funding sources. If the situation continues as it is, negative consequences are likely to increase. Furthermore, the following difficulties persist in establishing buffer zone councils and branch councils for Special Protected Areas (SPAs), as well as in the operations of currently functioning councils: ●    The representation of herders is low, and the active participation of selected herders is weak ●    The process for selecting council members is not optimal ●    The representation of women is low ●    The representation of youth is small There are several sources with conflicting data regarding the area coverage of State Protected Areas (SPA) and Local Protected Areas (LPA). According to the study "Current Status of Local Protected Areas and Policy Recommendations for Improving Management" conducted by the Sustainable Development Earth NGO: “As of July 20, 2020, a total of 1,748 sites covering 33,576,902 hectares for 17 different purposes under the category of local special needs land are registered in the Mining Computer Inventory System (MCIS) of the Mineral Resources and Petroleum Authority. This accounts for 21.4% of Mongolia's total territory. These belong to 17 types of special needs purposes. The inconsistencies in the quantitative data indicate a need to further strengthen coherence and alignment among the relevant legal instruments. Mongolia aims to place 30% of its total land area under protected area coverage by 2030. As of 2025, coverage has reached 21%, suggesting that the country is on track toward this target. progressItems.targetText: By 2030, Reduce the risk of extinction of threatened species and conserve genetic diversity
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: In Mongolia’s long-term strategic framework, the “Vision 2050” program and the Government Action Program include the following objective: “ Revise and establish updated Red Lists for animal and plant species, define and implement measures for the conservation of threatened species, conduct phased nationwide surveys of species distribution and populations, and create conditions for implementing appropriate management ”. Mongolia is actively implementing conservation measures in accordance with a variety of national laws, such as the Law on Environmental Protection , the Law on Fees for Natural Resources use , the Law on Environmental Impact Assessment , the Law on Animal , the Law on Natural Plants , the Law on Plant Health and Protection , and the Law on Genetic Resources , to reduce the extinction risk of threatened and endangered species and preserve genetic diversity. Relevant international treaties and conventions, including the Convention on Biological Diversity , the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) , the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals , and Ramsar Convention on Wetlands , also guide conservation activities. These national legal frameworks have been continuously amended and updated in response to the growing demands for environmental, economic, and societal conservation. For instance, the Law on Natural Plants was amended eight times between 1997 and 2024 , and the Law on Animal was amended seven times between 2015 and 2025 . These amendments were made in conjunction with ongoing endeavors to modernize the broader environmental legal framework. Legislation in Mongolia explicitly specifies the protection of specific species that are considered endangered. At present, the legal registry comprises the following: Plants : 133 vascular plants that are critically endangered and 355 vascular plants that are endangered; 11 lichens; 5 algae; 4 mosses; and 5 fungi. Animals : 31 species that are critically endangered and 70 species that are endangered. These data suggest that Mongolia has implemented a comprehensive legal framework to safeguard critically endangered and imperiled species on a national scale. In order to safeguard the genetic diversity of microorganisms, plants, and animals, the Government of Mongolia established a Gene Bank and, in 2022, implemented regulations to enhance the collection, documentation, preservation, protection, and distribution of genetic resources . The Law on the Livestock Genetic Resources was enacted in 2017 to protect livestock genetic resources and preserve genetic diversity. From 2019 to 2025, it was amended and updated. In addition, the Law on Seeds and Varieties of Cultivated Plant was revised and amended in 2021, establishing a critical legal framework for the sustainable use and conservation of plant genetic diversity. Since 2006, Mongolia has been utilizing the IUCN Red List categories and criteria to evaluate animal and plant species, in addition to enhancing the legal framework . This assessment serves as a critical foundation for determining the protection status of species, the level of threat, and the development of conservation plans. This made Mongolia the first country in Asia to evaluate vertebrate species. Consequently, Mongolia effectively completed the second national assessment and Red List compilation for amphibians, reptiles, mammals, and fish in 2025 , which included the assessment of their conservation status and evaluation. Mongolia has effectively expanded the network of protected areas, enhanced ecological integrity, created connectivity corridors, and strengthened their management in order to protect critically endangered and endangered species, their habitats, and distribution abundance. Nine linear infrastructure standards have been adopted and implemented to support the protection of migratory wild animals, and three plant species protection standards have been established. Ecological and socio-economic assessments were updated for 144 mammal species, 513 bird species, and 78 fish species in 2023 , and for 2,014 vascular plant species, 11 fungi species, and 25 moss species in 2022 . Under this objective, the Revenue from the Use of Natural Resources (RUNR) in 2025 amounted to MNT 200,496.0 million, with 25.8% of the total being allocated to environmental protection and ecosystem restoration. 43.3% of these expenditures were allocated to land protection, 33.7% to water resources, 11.3% to forests, and 11.6% to wildlife conservation activities . Approximately MNT 2.5 billion was allocated from the State Budget to the Gobi bear conservation program in 2024–2025 , and approximately MNT 100 million was spent in 2024 to evaluate the Saker Falcon's population size, distribution, and status . Furthermore, under specific projects: Over the course of eight years, the "Chuluut" initiative was awarded MNT 1.8 billion ; the "Sustainable Dry Steppe Landscapes and Biodiversity Conservation in Eastern Mongolia" project received USD 5,354,586 over a six-year period ; USD 10.688 million was allocated to the Ensure initiative over a six-year period .

To date, Mongolia has completed the evaluation of 1,928 vascular plant species, 559 moss species, 2,287 algae species, 1,079 lichen species, and 628 fungi species. Regional Red List assessments classify 126 of these species as Critically Endangered (CR), 353 as Endangered (EN), and 574 as Vulnerable (VU). Table 4.1. Of these, according to the regional Red List assessment, 1 species is Regionally Extinct (RE), 5 species are Critically Endangered (CR), 22 species are Endangered (EN), and 42 species are Vulnerable (VU). The evaluations have suffered since there isn't enough long-term monitoring data and not enough information on how many of specific species there are and where they are during the Red List assessments and efforts to protect genetic diversity. Research institutes still limit the sharing of data, and the creation of a single database system is still not finished. To effectively protect endangered species, it is essential to carry out long-term monitoring and scientific study focused on their range, population size, habitat, reproduction, genetic diversity, and threats. There are international treaties, national laws, standards, and methodological guidelines that make it illegal to kill endangered animals, but there are still not enough ways to check, evaluate, and enforce these regulations. The way established standards and procedures are applied in the field, how different organizations operate together, and how well the implementation is reviewed are all not good enough. This makes it harder to reach conservation goals in real life. Currently, there are restrictions on the ability to scientifically monitor the adherence to standards and systematically use research and monitoring results on threatened species to make decisions about policy and management. In Mongolia, research and conservation efforts for endangered species are mostly project-based and depend on funding from outside donors. There is yet no fully established way for the state budget to provide steady support for these efforts. Because of this, research and monitoring operations are generally short-term and not done all the time, which makes it challenging to measure genetic diversity and find long-term trends. So, national budget planning needs to periodically include money for study and protection of threatened species. Also, managing funds based on science-driven core initiatives needs to get better. Furthermore, the instability of competent personnel and the restricted access to laboratory and genetic research equipment hinder the capacity to do comprehensive and systematic investigations of genetic diversity. In this situation, the lack of unified monitoring and evaluation (M&E) indicators and integrated databases makes it challenging to properly assess, compare, and verify the implementation of approved standards, regulations, and conservation plans. Frequency of assessments: IUCN criteria say that reassessments should happen every five years, yet this doesn't happen. For example, the Snow Leopard Conservation Fund, in collaboration with the Environmental Office of Umnugobi Province, organized a discussion on “Reducing Conflicts between Snow Leopards and Herders”. Since 2020, the restocking and reintroduction program has been successfully implemented under the supervision of professional researchers .
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Implementation of National Target 4 has advanced primarily through large-scale Red List–aligned assessments and targeted conservation actions for threatened species and genetic resources. Across major taxonomic groups, Mongolia reports completed assessments for thousands of taxa using IUCN Red List categories and criteria, alongside the adoption of standards/methodological guidance and the initiation of species-focused measures (including in situ and ex situ efforts) to reduce extinction risk and support genetic resource conservation. Assessment quality and trend detection are constrained by data gaps, notably the lack of long-term monitoring and insufficient information on distribution and population size for a number of species. These limitations reduce the accuracy of Red List reassessments and complicate efforts to conserve genetic diversity effectively. Although legal and policy instruments, standards, and methodological documents have been adopted, both files highlight that monitoring, evaluation, and compliance in practice remain insufficient, including uneven application of approved standards and weak coordination for field-level delivery. For further implementation: (i) institutionalize science-based, long-term monitoring (distribution, population dynamics, habitat, breeding, genetic diversity, and threats) and restore a predictable cycle of reassessments; (ii) complete and operationalize integrated biodiversity databases and unified M&E indicators so that results are comparable, verifiable, and routinely used for adaptive management; (iii) strengthen field-level implementation and compliance, including inter-agency coordination and effectiveness tracking of approved plans/standards; and (iv) address enabling conditions through sustainable financing, targeted capacity support (including genetics-related capacity where feasible), and public awareness and coexistence measures—including community-based incentives and conflict-reduction approaches—so conservation goals translate into measurable outcomes on the ground.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: To reach this goal, the following steps have been taken: The Minister of Environment and Tourism signed Order A/208 on April 18, 2025, giving the green light to the National Plan for the Conservation of Critically Endangered and Endangered Species. As part of this plan, surveys were done on the size, abundance, and distribution of significant species, such as the Gobi bear ( Ursus arctos gobiensis ), Snow leopard ( Panthera uncia ), Przewalski’s horse ( Equus ferus przewalskii ), Khulan ( Equus hemionus ), Argali ( Ovis ammon ), Musk deer ( Moschus moschiferus ), Mongolian saiga ( Saiga tatarica mongolica ), Bactrian Camel ( Camelus ferus ), and Red deer ( Cervus elaphus ). A new breeding center was built outside of the Bactrian camel's natural habitat to help the population recover. These centers now have breeding herds of about 40 animals each, which helps the population develop and the species recover . The biological resources of about 300 species of vascular plants were looked at in the Khangai , Khentei, and Mongolian Daura regions as part of the Government Action Programs 2020–2024 and 2024–2028. Additionally, genetic, morphological, and distribution research was performed on highly endangered plant species, including Adonis mongolica, Fritillaria dagana, Saussurea involucrata , and Allium altaicum , leading to the formulation of conservation recommendations based on the results. Under the “Sustainable Landscape and Biodiversity Conservation of the Dry Steppe of Eastern Mongolia” project (2021–2026) , conservation actions were implemented for critically endangered and endangered species such as the Mongolian gazelle, goitered gazelle, and white-naped crane. The " Ensuring Mongolia's Native Ecosystem Resilience and Stability (Ensure)" project (2019–2025) also preserved the habitats of severely endangered and endangered species such the musk deer ( Moschus moschiferus ), red deer ( Cervus elaphus ), Mongolian marmot ( Marmota sibirica ) , and Rheum ribes . Between 2018 and 2025 , the “Future of Snow Leopard Landscapes” Project implemented by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) focused on protecting the habitat of snow leopards in the Darviin Mountains and Khasagt Khairkhan areas of Gobi-Altai Province, increasing the populations of prey species, and reducing illegal hunting and wildlife trade. Under the project, activities were successfully carried out with the involvement of local communities and herders, including the deployment of livestock Bankhar dogs, installation of wildlife-friendly enclosures, implementation of sustainable pasture management, protection of springs and water sources, and reintroduction of marmots. These measures reduced livestock losses and increased populations of wild animals, leading to improved snow leopard habitat, enhanced tourism opportunities, and a comprehensive program supporting sustainable local development, community livelihoods, and ecosystem connectivity. Under the “Chuluut Tul” Project , implemented to restore fish populations, over an eight-year period, 3,030,000 juvenile lenok and Mongolian grayling ( Thymallus brevirostris ) were bred and released into their natural habitats. Since 2019, M ongolian and Swedish researchers have conducted the first study of Mongolian grayling migration in Khar Us Lake and have been working to develop policies to protect the habitats and migratory corridors of migratory fish species, including taimen, lenok and pike in the Nomrog and Onon river basins. The “eZagas” electronic system , which consolidates information on fishing permits and approved fishing zones, has been introduced and implemented in 31 soums of Khentii and Khuvsgul provinces . Within the framework of snow leopard conservation activities, organizations including the Snow Leopard Trust, Snow Leopard Mongolia Center, WWF Mongolia Program, Wildlife Conservation Society, and the Institute of Biology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, together with local communities and herder cooperatives, have been implementing initiatives to strengthen local capacities, support livelihoods, and enhance knowledge and awareness.

reportedActions: Mongolia's accession to the International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC) in 1997 was one of the primary measures implemented to enhance its capacity for the identification, monitoring, impact assessment, and response to invasive species, as well as to prevent the adverse impacts of invasive alien species. Mongolia subsequently developed its National Security Concept in 2010 , which includes a provision that states "a system shall be established to prevent genetic impacts on biodiversity and to ensure control when introducing alien animal, plant, and microorganism species". Mongolia has endeavored to investigate alien animal and plant species that are present in the country and to establish enabling conditions to prevent the introduction, establishment, and spread of invasive alien species within the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) since 2015. At present, the Law on Environmental Protection , Law on Natural Plants , Law on Animals , Law on Permits , and Law on Offences regulate issues related to invasive species. Furthermore, the introduction of 35 species of plant pests and insects, 11 weed species, and 2 rodent species across the Mongolian border has been officially prohibited by Order No. A-100 of the Minister of Food , Agriculture, and Light Industry (2018), and this regulation continues to be in effect. Also, the "Guidelines for the Import Regulation System for Plant Health" (MNS ISPM 20:2024) are now in use to stop quarantine pests from entering and moving through Mongolia. Five new phytosanitary standards have been authorized to date as part of the framework of activities to translate and adapt International Standards for Phytosanitary Measures (ISPMs). Several projects have been successfully implemented at the national level to inventory invasive species, develop national lists, and determine their distribution. These projects include "Compilation of a List of Invasive Animal and Plant Species Occurring in Mongolia, Development of Recommendations, and Publication of a Handbook" (2019) and "Study of Invasive Plant and Animal Species in the Central Region of Mongolia" (2024). These efforts have led to the discovery of 154 alien plant species . The aimags of Darkhan-Uul (130 species), Selenge (119 species), Ulaanbaatar (110 species), and Tuv (102 species) are the most widely distributed agriculturally developed regions that contain alien plant species. Furthermore, a total of 18 alien fungal species , 5 alien mite species, 27 alien insect species , 13 alien fish species, and 5 alien mammal species have been documented throughout the country. The absence of impact-based classification systems and risk assessment adversely affects policy development and decision-making. 3. progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Transporting imported food and agricultural products across borders and customs checkpoints unintentionally introduces the majority of alien mite and insect species. For instance, wheat imported from Kazakhstan and the United States between 2000 and 2005 introduced the common storage mite (Glycyphagus destructor) , a quarantine pest that is domestically regulated. In addition, the mealworm (Tenebrio molitor) has been deliberately introduced for the purpose of feeding domesticated animals and is presently bred and traded through pet shops. Additionally, the distribution ranges of the gypsy moth (Lymantria dispar) and the Siberian silk moth (Dendrolimus sibiricus) are being extended. Some of the 13 alien fish species recorded in Mongolia  were intentionally introduced for aquaculture purposes. For example, natural omul (Coregonus migratorius) was added to Lake Khuvsgul and Lake Ulaagchnii Khar; peled (Coregonus peled) was added to Lower Tsagaan Lake, Targan Lake, Ulaagchnii Khar Lake, and Naiman Lake; and Northern When these alien fish species are established without effective control, they become excessively abundant, resulting in multiple negative impacts on native fish species at the ecological, genetic, and ecosystem levels. For example, the population viability of the native species is at risk due to the hybridization of the alien species peled (Coregonus peled) with the critically endangered (CR) whitefish (Coregonus pidschian) in Mongolia . Five alien mammal species have been documented in Mongolia : the house mouse (Mus musculus), American mink (Neovison vison), muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus), brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), and raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides). The spread and growth of these non-native mammals, which can easily adapt and reproduce quickly, create several dangers for the ecosystem and the survival of local mammal species. For instance, the muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus), a semi-aquatic mammal that is indigenous to North America, was deliberately introduced during the 1950s and 1960s for the purpose of fur cultivation. The direct and indirect impacts of this species on native species are underscored by the significant numbers of non-target wildlife that are captured by the traps set for it, including rainbow trout and other animals.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: To achieve this objective, the following measures have been implemented. Mongolia has established a legal framework that allows for the integration of provisions related to alien species into national legislation by adhering to the IPPC in 1997 and the CBD in 2015. All aimags contain 29 of the 154 recorded alien plant species, which are considered invasive. Darkhan-Uul (130 species), Selenge (119 species), Ulaanbaatar (110 species), and Tuv (102 species) are agriculturally developed regions that are particularly replete with alien plants. Additionally, Mongolia has documented 74–85 alien plant species by consulting international databases    that document alien animals, plants, and microorganisms. For instance, the iNaturalist platform has collected data on 80 alien plant species, corresponding to 1,085 plots . Currently, the National University of Mongolia (UBU) herbarium contains 194 herbariums of desiccated specimens of 62 alien plant species . The following plant species have been collected multiple times: Setaria viridis (43 herbariums), Cannabis sativa (29), Amaranthus retroflexus (19), Xanthium strumarium (13), Brassica campestris (11), Chloris virgata (11). These collections serve as a crucial foundation for the development of policy and management planning, as well as for the further ecological and biological studies of alien species.

reportedActions: Mongolia is progressively implementing international agreements and domestic legislation, standards, and economic regulations aimed at reducing pollution that adversely affects biodiversity and improving the management of hazardous waste and chemicals. Mongolia has acceded to and assumed obligations under key international instruments, including the “ Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal ” (1996), the “Rotterdam Convention” on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade ” (1999), the “Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants” (2003), the “Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety to the Convention on Biological Diversity” (2002), and the “Minamata Convention on Mercury” (2015). The legal basis for reducing pollution has been established through sectoral legislation, implementing regulations, and relevant standards and technical regulations, including “ the Law on Environmental Protection” , “the Law on Waste” , “the Law on Toxic and Hazardous Chemicals” , “the National Programme on Soil Protection and Land Degradation Reduction” , and the following national standards: “Soil quality-Maximum permissible levels of pollutants in soil” (MNS 5850), “Plastics-Guidelines for the recovery and recycling of plastic waste” (MNS ISO 15270:2024), “Plastics-Evaluation of the effectiveness of fungal growth inhibitory compounds in plastic formulations” (MNS ISO 16869:2024), and “Wastewater discharged into sewer networks-General requirements” (MNS 6561:2024), as well as the Regulation on the system, structure and data submission procedures for the National Integrated Waste Information Database, and the Regulation on the collection, sorting, transport, recycling, recovery, disposal and landfilling of non-hazardous waste, among others. Key priorities include: (i) strengthening waste data and control systems; (ii) reducing plastic waste at source; (iii) promoting safer and rational use of pesticides and fertilizers; and (iv) applying economic instruments and pre-treatment requirements to reduce water pollution. As part of efforts to improve waste management, a regulation on the national integrated waste information database [11] was approved, which has strengthened data collection and improved the reporting system. In addition, Government Resolution №189 (2018) prohibited the import, production, and use of single-use plastic bags with a thickness of “0.035 mm or less” starting from “1 March 2019”, representing a key step to curb plastic waste at the source . Within the framework of chemicals and pesticide regulation, an electronic system is being operated to digitalize the baseline registration of toxic and hazardous chemicals, reference information, and the registry of permitted entities . By the joint order of the Minister of Environment and Tourism and the Minister of Food, Agriculture and Light Industry dated “26 February 2024” (Joint Orders A/96, A/104 and A/81), the list of pesticides and chemical fertilizers permitted for agricultural use and their application rates were approved, and regulatory measures to reduce risks associated with use have begun to be implemented . The database of toxic and hazardous chemicals, including prohibited chemicals, as well as hazard reference information, has been systematized and digitized, alongside strengthened controls over the use and consumption of such substances, the disposal of containers and packaging, and the information related to substances subject to special permits issued to enterprises and organizations. To reduce water pollution, the “Law on Water Contamination Fees” established an economic “polluter pays” mechanism requiring polluters to pay charges, and arrangements have been made to enable payment through the national e-service channel (e-mongolia). Furthermore, Government Resolution №53 of “3 March 2021” approved and initiated the implementation of the “Industrial Wastewater Pre-treatment Plan”, which sets out phased measures to reduce the pollution load from industrial wastewater. To improve water quality and wastewater management in Ulaanbaatar, the Government of Mongolia, in partnership with the Millennium Challenge Corporation, is implementing a “350 million USD Compact II” that includes developing a new water source, establishing a wastewater recycling facility, and undertaking policy reforms to strengthen long-term sector sustainability. In addition, under policies aimed at protecting headwater areas and aquatic ecosystems that generate river flows, 44.7% of the total headwater catchment area had been brought under state special protection as of 2019.

progressItems.progressSummary: Investments have improved solid-waste management infrastructure and services in provincial centers and Ulaanbaatar, including sanitary landfill capacity and facilities for construction and demolition waste processing, with additional landfill planning in key tourism areas. Monitoring indicates continuing pollution risks (e.g., pesticide residues and contaminated agricultural land), and research has confirmed microplastic pollution in Lake Khuvsgul and the Tuul River basin. Recycling rates remain low and plastic waste is increasing. Way forward: strengthen enforcement and risk-based monitoring; expand source separation and recycling; and apply “polluter pays” and extended producer responsibility approaches supported by digital tracking and multi-stakeholder engagement.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: With grant support from the Japan Fund for Poverty Reduction (JFPR), the “Solid Waste Management” (G9206) project established and commissioned core waste infrastructure in provincial centers, including centralized waste facilities, recyclable collection points, and compaction/transfer equipment in Sukhbaatar, Darkhan-Uul, Uvurkhangai, and Govi-Altai aimag centers, thereby improving the quality of solid waste services. In Ulaanbaatar, a sanitary landfill with a capacity to receive 8.5 million tons of waste in an environmentally sound manner was developed, and a construction and demolition waste processing plant with an annual capacity of 170,000 tons was established. In addition, under the Asian Development Bank project on sustainable tourism development, plans were prepared to construct landfill facilities in tourism areas, including Lake Khövsgöl and the Onon-Balj National Park, further strengthening solid waste management infrastructure and service delivery. To improve the financial sustainability of waste services, a methodology for calculating waste service fees and a legal guidance manual for the sector were developed. Training for public inspectors was also organized, strengthening local-level oversight and implementation capacity. Under the SWITCH-Asia Programme, the “Sustainable Plastic Recycling in Mongolia (SPRIM)” project supported policy implementation on the 3R principle and sustainable production and consumption by establishing national standards for plastic recycling, including MNS ISO 15270:2024 and MNS ISO 16869:2024. Evidence on chemical pollution pressures has expanded through baseline research and monitoring. In 2022, the Institute of Plant Protection conducted a study on “Determining the quality and residues of pesticides and fertilizers,” analyzing residues in crop products and soil samples. Residues were detected in 30% of imported vegetable samples, and 10% exceeded permissible limits. The 2023 land damage report recorded damage on 82,774.5 ha of cropland nationwide, of which 7,542.1 ha (9%) was reported as contaminated by chemicals-demonstrating tangible pressure from chemical pollution in soils and providing baseline evidence for agricultural chemical risk assessment and monitoring. To progressively reduce wastewater pollution and associated environmental impacts, protect overall water resources, and promote safe water reuse, “the Law on Water Contamination Fees” was adopted on 17 May 2012, with amendments introduced in 2015, 2017, 2019, 2022, and 2024, alongside approval of necessary regulatory instruments-indicating that wastewater regulation and pollution-reduction investments are ongoing. To strengthen implementation, a joint order dated 3 September 2025 ( A/705 and A/205 ) approved “benchmark pollutant concentrations” for entities discharging less than 50 m³/day of wastewater. Under the second compact agreement between the Government of Mongolia and the Millennium Challenge Corporation (Compact II), a wastewater recycling plant has been constructed as part of the “Ulaanbaatar Water Supply Expansion Program.” In addition, the “Project to expand, rehabilitate, and newly construct provincial wastewater treatment plants” is being implemented in Bayan-Ölgii, Uvs, Zavkhan, and Govisümber aimags, with construction works, client supervision, and testing activities underway. The zoning and coverage of protected areas for safeguarding aquatic ecosystems from pollution have expanded. In 2023, 7,202,380.7 ha equivalent to 50% of “ headwater catchment areas and surface water resources ” were brought under state special protection. Mapping and methodological work developed by the World-Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) has provided an important basis for delineating pollution-protection zones for water bodies and wetlands. Baseline data on pollution risks continue to grow, and research findings are emerging. For example, a study in Lake Khövsgöl identified 20,264 microplastic particles per km², confirming the risk of microplastic pollution and serving as a baseline indicator for future monitoring. Research in the Tuul River Basin has also examined the impacts of plastic, microplastic, and construction polystyrene foam waste , indicating potential accumulation in water, sediments, and microorganisms and associated adverse effects. Nationally, approximately 2.2 million tons of recyclable (secondary raw material) waste are generated annually, of which 1.4 million tons are generated in Ulaanbaatar. Nationwide, only 3–5% of total waste is recycled, while the recycling rate in Ulaanbaatar is 8.9%. In recent years, the volume of plastic waste has increased year by year, and its environmental impacts have continued to rise. Plastic product waste accounts for 26.6% of recycled waste, underscoring the need to intensify reduction and recycling policies. Strengthening the legal framework to operationalize the principles of “producer responsibility” and “polluter pays”-including take-back mechanisms for single-use plastic packaging through producers, importers, and recyclable collection points-is essential. Going forward, institutionalizing monitoring for microplastics, chemicals, and soil pollution; harmonizing national-level databases and reporting standards; and combining market-based incentives, digital monitoring, and multi-stakeholder participation will increase the effectiveness of achieving the target.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: Under a project implemented by the Institute of Chemistry and Chemical Technology, Mongolian Academy of Sciences in cooperation with the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, with funding from the United Nations Environment Programme, a training and seminar was held on 20 October 2023 with the participation of more than 90 national and local representatives. This activity strengthened knowledge and capacity on the classification, analysis, and oversight of hazardous waste. The database of toxic and hazardous chemicals has been digitalized, improving transparency and providing a foundation for strengthening permitting and compliance processes. In 2023, 196 enterprises and organizations obtained special permits for toxic and hazardous chemicals through the “e-Mongolia” system. With financing from the EU SWITCH-Asia II Programme, the project “ Ensuring Sustainable Plastic Recycling in Mongolia ” was implemented to reduce waste generation in target areas and improve waste management through “ source separation and recycling ”, including by establishing a sustainably operating central hub. Recycling companies actively participating in the project collected and recycled a total of 30,745 tons of waste during 2020–2024. The designation of “World Environment Day 2025” as a call for solutions to plastic pollution is further contributing momentum to achieving this target. By the joint order of the Minister of Environment and Tourism, the Minister of Food, Agriculture and Light Industry, and the Minister of Health dated 26 February 2024 (Joint Orders A/96, A/104 and A/81), the list and application rates of 252 types of pesticides used in agriculture (57 insecticides, 128 herbicides, 62 fungicides, and 5 rodenticides) and 62 types of chemical fertilizers were approved. This provides a policy basis for standardizing pesticide and fertilizer use in agriculture and reducing risks of soil and water pollution arising from over-application. Based on the results of surface water quality monitoring conducted during 2021–2023 at 193 monitoring points across 94 rivers and 19 lakes nationwide, 28–45% of the monitored rivers and lakes were classified as “very clean”, 43–62% as “clean”, 5–12% as “slightly polluted”, 2–3% as “polluted”, 1–2% as “dirty”, and 2–3% as “heavily polluted”. Sites classified as “polluted” included Songino, Khadan Khiasaa and Altanbulag along the Tuul River; Khiagt in the Selenge River basin; and the Khangal River in Orkhon Province. Sites classified as “slightly polluted” included Shuvuun Fabrik, Selbe and Dundgol on the Tuul River system; Khangal and Chingel (Erdenet); and areas around Lun along the Tuul River. Major sources of pollution include the Central Wastewater Treatment Plant in Songino (impacting the Tuul River), cross-border sources affecting the Khiagt River, and wastewater treatment facilities affecting the Khangal River. Sediment cleaning works have been organized along the Tuul River channel downstream of the central wastewater treatment plant. Efforts are also underway to recycle effluent from the central wastewater treatment plant and reuse it for industrial purposes at Thermal Power Plants III and IV, including through construction of a wastewater recycling and supply facility together with the associated conveyance infrastructure. In addition, projects such as “Protecting Ganga Lake from pollution and drying”, “Assessment of pollution risks to the ecosystem of Lake Khövsgöl” and “Phase II implementation to protect Ögii Lake from pollution and drying and to improve inflows” are being implemented successfully. With support from the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) under the “100, 1000, 10000” initiative, a “Unified methodology for fencing and protecting spring sources” was developed, and the sources of 137 springs were fenced nationwide. This has delivered direct results by reducing contamination of local water sources and protecting habitats of small aquatic ecosystems. The air quality monitoring network has been expanded to all 21 aimags, with automatic monitoring stations installed. In Ulaanbaatar, the use of processed coal for household heating has contributed to a reduction in air pollution.

It also ratified the Kyoto Protocol on 15 December 1999 and the Paris Agreement on 21 September 2016. In implementing the Paris Agreement, Mongolia updated its “Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0)”, specifying sector-specific targets and measures for mitigation and adaptation. The document sets a target to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 30.3% by 2035 and includes measures to increase carbon sequestration through expanding forests, the land sector, and green spaces. The Government-approved document on the “NDC Targets for Implementing the Paris Agreement” was adopted by Government of Mongolia through Resolution №407 in 2019. On adaptation policy, the “National Adaptation Plan (NAP 2024–2030)” translates the objective of “climate-resilient development” into implementation by defining sectoral risk assessments, priority actions, implementation arrangements, and financing needs. To implement mitigation, increase carbon sequestration, and strengthen climate change adaptation, Mongolia has established and is applying the legal and regulatory framework through “the Law on Environmental Protection” , “the Law on Air” , “the Law on Water” , “the Law on Forest” , “the Law on Land” , and other relevant legislation. To reduce disaster risk and prevent the emergence of new risks-by improving hazard and vulnerability reduction, prevention, preparedness, response, recovery, and resilience-the “Mid-Term Strategy for Implementing the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction in Mongolia” has been approved and implemented since 2017. In accordance with the Law on Disaster Protection, aimags, soums, the capital city, and districts develop and implement disaster risk reduction program and disaster protection plans. In addition, the procedure for conducting disaster risk assessments was revised and approved under Government Resolution №190 (2020), improving provisions for carrying out risk assessments at defined intervals and as conditions require. Under nature-based solutions and efforts to increase carbon sinks, Mongolia is implementing national initiatives such as the One Billion Trees initiative, promoting afforestation, restoration, and expansion of green areas in alignment with targets to enhance carbon sequestration. “The Mongolian Nature Heritage Fund””, which implements the “Eternal Mongolia” long-term conservation financing program, is investing in biodiversity conservation, climate change mitigation, and other conservation priorities, generating multiple co-benefits. Based on mitigation results for 2020-2024, the evaluation of NDC 2.0 indicates that greenhouse gas emissions declined steadily as a result of measures implemented in both the energy and non-energy sectors.
