progressItems.progressSummary: Under National Target 7, Mongolia has strengthened the foundation for improving climate policies and strategies by enhancing the framework for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, increasing carbon sequestration, and improving adaptive capacity. An implementation action plan for the Nationally Determined Contribution ( NDC ) for 2021–2025 (comprising 8 objectives and 75 measures) was approved. Together with improvements to the adaptation policy through the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) and enhancements to the greenhouse gas inventory and reporting system, these steps have strengthened the institutional basis for integrating climate objectives into sectoral planning, measuring implementation progress, and reporting results.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: In the forest sector, a wide range of measures are being implemented to mitigate climate change and increase greenhouse gas removals. For example, during 2021–2023, afforestation activities covered more than 11,000 ha, and by October 2025 a total of 117 million trees had been planted nationwide. Measures to prevent and combat forest fires and strengthen response capacity contributed to reducing the area of forest affected by fires by 23.5 thousand ha, while actions to control forest pests were undertaken across 250,000 ha. In addition, the volume of illegally harvested and confiscated timber decreased by 15.49%, from 695.2 m³ in 2019–2020 to 587.5 m³ in 2021–2022 . According to calculations under the forest-sector assessment of the NDC, the level of forest-related greenhouse gas removals in 2024 slightly exceeded the target level (by 4.33%) and was 4.46% higher than the baseline scenario. Figure. Forest greenhouse gas removals under the “enhanced sequestration” scenario and the assessed level, expressed as a percentage and compared with the baseline scenario. As the baseline for disaster risk assessment and early warning information has been strengthened, conditions have been created to improve preparedness, prevention, and the organization of response measures for risks such as drought and dzud. By Government Resolution No. 355 (2017), the “Mid-Term Strategy for Implementing the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction in Mongolia” was approved through 2030 and is being implemented in three phases. The “Regulation on Conducting Disaster Risk Assessments” was approved by Government Resolution No. 63 (2018) and, in line with amendments to the Law on Disaster Protection, was revised and updated by Government Resolution No. 190 (2020). Based on the principles and requirements of the MNS ISO 31000:2020 Risk Management—Guidelines standard, as well as the key principles, scope, and required indicators for disaster risk assessment, the “Guideline for Conducting Disaster Risk Assessments” was developed for 10 major types of disasters that commonly occur in Mongolia and its revised version was approved by Order No. 68 (2021). In addition, under the ADAPT project, a “Disaster Risk Management” handbook was developed and delivered to local authorities and relevant specialists to strengthen capacities for disaster risk reduction, minimizing losses during disaster events, and taking timely response actions. While Mongolia has established the policy foundation for responding to climate change and achieved initial tangible progress in reducing emissions, increasing carbon sequestration, and improving adaptive capacity, challenges remain. These include constraints in financing; limited detailed, subnational-level data on greenhouse gas emissions and carbon sinks; and insufficient technical expertise and human resources at aimag and soum levels, as well as coordination issues in implementation. Going forward, combining ecosystem-based solutions—such as restoring forests, rangelands, and wetlands to reduce climate impacts through natural processes—with digital monitoring (including satellite and sensor-based monitoring of emissions and improved risk assessment for adaptation) will enhance the effectiveness of implementing this target. Over the past 80 years, Mongolia’s average air temperature has increased by 2.46°C, which is about two to three times higher than the global average over the past 100 years. Due to its geographic location, fragile ecosystems, livelihood patterns, and economic structure, Mongolia is highly exposed and vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, and faces elevated socio-ecological risks. Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of drought and dzud, surface evaporation, the number of hot days, and aridity, contributing to desertification and rangeland ecosystem degradation. As a result, livestock losses are increasing, herder livelihoods are deteriorating, and rural poverty and rural-to-urban migration are rising. In Mongolia’s context, poverty and migration are largely rural in origin, and climate change is a significant contributing factor. High dependence on climate-sensitive conditions and increased vulnerability indicates a heightened risk of exposure to future natural hazards. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the legal and regulatory framework on climate change and to establish the legal, financial, and institutional arrangements for planning and financing climate change adaptation for the population, society, vulnerable groups, and economic sectors.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: With financing from the International Climate Initiative of the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action, the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ) is implementing the project “Support for the Paris Agreement Implementation (SPA).” In the context of advancing and updating Mongolia’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), the project is supporting the Government of Mongolia in developing a document roadmap and in strengthening sectoral mitigation targets across five sectors. Mongolia’s “First Biennial Update Report” is a report that communicates to the institutions of the global community Mongolia’s efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions following the submission on 24 September 2015 of the document “Mongolia’s Intended Nationally Determined Contribution (INDC) to the global effort to mitigate climate change” to the Convention. The project “Improving Adaptive Capacity and Risk Management of Rural Communities in Mongolia ( ADAPT )” is implementing policies, projects, and programmes aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving climate risk assessment and monitoring, protecting and restoring vulnerable ecosystems such as water, rangelands, and forests, strengthening disaster risk management and early warning systems, and enhancing the adaptive capacity of local communities. In the area of afforestation and increasing carbon sequestration, the President of Mongolia, Ukhnaa Khurelsukh, issued a decree on 4 October 2021 to launch the One Billion Trees National Movement, followed by Government-level measures to organize implementation. According to official information, an inventory and stock assessment of nurseries conducted in 2023 covered 452 nurseries and identified 62,978,816 seedlings and saplings available for planting, indicating increased capacity to scale up afforestation. Information from 2024 further indicates that seed and seedling stocks have continued to grow, strengthening preparedness to meet afforestation targets, with the aim of increasing carbon sequestration through afforestation and restoration. Because Mongolia’s rangelands cover a large share of the national territory, effective management has significant potential to increase soil organic carbon (SOC). Reducing rangeland degradation and restoring rangelands can therefore serve as a solution to enhance carbon sequestration. In this context, under the FAO SCALA Programme, policy recommendations were developed on increasing rangeland carbon sequestration and on domestic market considerations. One of the fastest and most effective approaches to strengthen adaptive capacity is to improve risk assessment and early warning. Mongolia’s overall disaster risk assessment coverage for administrative units was 8% in 2016; as the legal framework and institutional arrangements improved, this rose to 71% in 2019 and reached 100% in 2020, indicating rapid expansion of risk information and planning coverage. The National Agency for Meteorology and Environmental Monitoring (NAMEM) conducts continuous monitoring of weather and hazardous events. Since 2010, permafrost observations have been carried out at 13 sites, expanded to 27 sites (including 14 additional sites since 2013), and baseline studies on data collection and processing have been conducted in collaboration with the Institute of Geography and Geoecology, Mongolian Academy of Sciences. Under early warning services, the “Tsag Agaar” mobile application has been available to the public since September 2019. In a study of the 2023–2024 dzud , 81% of surveyed herder households reported having received dzud and weather early warnings in advance, demonstrating progress. Due to historically high reliance on raw coal for urban heating, a policy was implemented in Ulaanbaatar to prohibit household-level use of raw coal from 15 May 2019 and replace it with briquetted fuel. Research articles (including on particulate matter concentrations) report that measurable improvements were observed after the ban, indicating that policy measures can yield impacts within a relatively short period.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, reduce ecosystem degradation by supporting the development of sustainable, highly productive forestry and agriculture, while introducing nature-based practices.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: Sustainable and productive production—particularly livestock production—is fundamentally based on rangelands, which cover more than 70 percent of Mongolia’s total territory. These rangelands play a critical role in conserving and supporting biodiversity. At the initiative of Mongolia, a country with rich traditional knowledge rooted in thousands of years of nomadic livestock husbandry in harmony with nature, the United Nations General Assembly proclaimed 2026 as the “International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists.” This represents an important step in recognizing the sector’s significance at the international level. Mongolia’s long- and medium-term policy documents—including Vision 2050, the New Recovery Policy, the Government of Mongolia Action Program 2024–2028, the Billion Trees National Movement, the White Gold National Movement, the Fourth Atar Campaign, and the Food Supply and Food Security Policy—emphasize the development of environmentally friendly, sustainable, and productive agriculture. The foundation of sustainable and productive agriculture, particularly livestock production, is rangeland, which covers more than 70 percent of Mongolia’s total territory . In this context, and in recognition of Mongolia’s abundant traditional knowledge derived from practicing nomadic pastoralism in harmony with nature for thousands of years, the United Nations General Assembly, at Mongolia’s initiative, proclaimed 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists . Rangeland degradation leads to the impoverishment of plant communities, soil degradation, and the loss of wildlife habitats. Rangeland ecosystems play a critical role in conserving and supporting biodiversity. In Mongolia, the legal and regulatory framework for rangeland protection, responsible and sustainable use of rangeland in line with its carrying capacity, and the regulation of livestock numbers and structure is being strengthened. For example, amendments to the Law on Land were introducing provisions under Article 58 that mandate a state-level assessment and certification of land condition and quality every 5 years, based on a unified methodology. Furthermore, amendments to Article 52 , paragraph 2 of the Law on Land, adopted on June 5, 2024, legally established the contractual use of four-season rangelands in accordance with rangeland carrying capacity. This has become an important mechanism for limiting rangeland degradation and conserving biodiversity. In 2020, the Law on Livestock Head Tax was adopted, establishing a legal framework for imposing a tax on livestock numbers and allocating tax revenues for rangeland protection and restoration. The Strategic Plan for the Breeding of the Five Livestock Species , approved in 2020 and currently under implementation, has placed livestock breeding and selection on a more scientific and controlled footing. This has laid the foundation for shifting livestock production from a focus on quantity to quality. As a result, productivity per animal has increased, livestock numbers can be better aligned with rangeland carrying capacity, and conditions for improving rangeland health have been established. In the context of the sustainable use of the environment, rangeland, feed resources, and water supply, as well as the regulation and monitoring of chemical inputs used in livestock production, Mongolia has adopted and is implementing the MNS 6891:2020 Standard “Requirements for the Implementation of Responsible Nomadic Pastoral Practices”. Compliance is monitored through an electronic tracking system. Monitoring of rangeland ecosystem state has been conducted, and Rangeland State Reports were published in 2015, 2018, and 2020. These reports have enabled an objective assessment of long-term changes in rangeland state, the classification of rangeland recovery potential, and the development of accurate rangeland use and management strategies. A Methodology for Determining Rangeland Carrying Capacity [1] has been approved, under which the Institute of Meteorology, Hydrology and Environment calculates winter and spring rangeland carrying capacity at the bagh (subdistrict) level. These calculations are based on data including rangeland productivity, livestock numbers, rangeland area, and the duration of rangeland use. Crop production is a strategic sector for meeting the food needs of the population; however, it is also one of the sectors that exerts significant pressure on the environment. Soil degradation, water pollution, and the improper use of chemical substances are among the main drivers of biodiversity loss. Therefore, introducing environmentally friendly and sustainable technologies in agricultural areas is a key approach to simultaneously ensuring biodiversity conservation and food security. Mongolia has been implementing a number of measures and has achieved notable progress in this regard. For example, amendments to the Law on Plant Health and Plant Protection were adopted on June 5, 2024, establishing a legal framework for the reporting and traceability of the use of plant protection agents. In addition, the National Program on Soil Protection and Reduction of Land Degradation was approved and implemented, focusing on reducing soil degradation and restoring soil quality. By Order No. 34 of February 22, 2019, issued by the Minister of Construction and Urban Development , methodological guidelines were approved for the assessment and certification of the condition and quality of agricultural land. Decisions have also been taken to establish protective forest belts and to implement agroforestry practices on croplands . Furthermore, research activities have commenced to intensify efforts to quantify carbon dioxide emissions from brown soils in agricultural fields. [1] https://downloads.1212.mn/1616736153165.pdf

progressItems.progressSummary: Of the total area covered by 1,520 rangeland monitoring study sites, 69 percent show changes in the species composition of dominant rangeland plants compared to their optimal condition, and rangeland carrying capacity has been exceeded in 215 soums. Overgrazing is particularly severe in the forest-steppe and steppe zones [1]. Rangelands are becoming drier, with truly xerophytic plant species characteristic of dry steppe conditions accounting for 43–69 percent of dominant rangeland vegetation [2], indicating an intensification of aridification processes and an increased risk of soil erosion and degradation. On the positive side, approximately 80 percent of degraded rangelands have the potential to recover naturally if appropriate, science-based grazing practices are introduced and herd management is improved [3]. In order to enhance soil fertility and moisture in croplands and to introduce eco-friendly technologies, green fallow practices using 12 types of crops have been implemented [4], resulting in the development of new soil improvement technologies. Soil fertility levels and degrees of erosion in agricultural fields were assessed through analysis conducted at 200 monitoring sites [4]. In addition, studies were carried out to bring abandoned cropland in selected soums of Tuv and Bulgan aimags back into production by analyzing the chemical and mechanical composition of the soils. This approach helps avoid the expansion of cultivation into natural and uncultivated lands and prevents changes in land-use classification, thereby reducing the risk of habitat degradation and loss of biodiversity. At the same time, Mongolia faces numerous challenges in achieving this target. Although policies aim to shift livestock production from quantity to quality, align livestock numbers with rangeland carrying capacity, and improve rangeland status, implementation remains insufficient. As of 2024, the total livestock number in Mongolia reached 57.6 million head [5], doubling compared to 1990, and continues to show an upward trend. Sheep and goats, which are relatively low in productivity, account for 82.3 percent of the total herd. The imbalance in herd structure, particularly the doubling of the goat population compared to 1990, has had a serious negative impact on rangeland productivity and state. Of the total cultivated land area, 61.4% of soils are severely eroded, 34.9% are moderately eroded, and 3.7% are slightly eroded , resulting in a decline in soil fertility indicators. According to the Environmental Performance Index (EPI) released by Yale University in 2024, agricultural productivity measured by potential yield per hectare, remains relatively low; in 2024, Mongolia scored 33.2 points, ranking 163rd among countries worldwide [6]. Also, Mongolia recorded high levels of inefficient use of nitrogen and phosphorus fertilizers and an increased risk of pesticide pollution. Due to fertilizer subsidies, soil characteristics, and moisture deficits, the inefficient use of chemical N and P fertilizers remains high (EPI Sustainable Nitrogen Management Index: 0.2 points, ranked 178th; phosphorus use efficiency: 28.2 points, ranked 164th. Although the legal framework for reporting and tracking the use of plant protection products is improving, the risk of pesticide pollution has increased since 2015, with an EPI score of 88.1 points [6], ranked 14th. In Mongolia, detailed environmental impact assessments have not been conducted for cropland, and as a result, areas of high biodiversity value within agricultural land-use categories are not being excluded from use and placed under protection based on comprehensive ecological, social, and economic studies. progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: To overcome these challenges and move toward improvement: Strengthen pasture-carrying-capacity-based accountability systems: Enhance contractual rangeland use arrangements with primary herder groups; regulate livestock numbers and herd composition in line with carrying capacity; and conduct post-use monitoring and evaluation of rangeland conditions. Advance the transition “from quantity to quality”: Ensure effective implementation of breeding strategies; increase the quality and value of livestock-derived products; and maintain livestock numbers at an optimal level without reducing herders’ incomes. Promote the transition to sustainable cropping systems: Phase out bare fallow practices and gradually expand conservation agriculture approaches, including cover crops/green manure, crop rotation with perennial species, and zero tillage; intensify soil restoration and erosion control measures. Reduce nutrient and pesticide risks: Apply fertilizers and pesticides at the required dose and precise location using smart technologies; and improve traceability systems. Minimize land-use change: Limit the conversion of fallow and natural lands; reduce land-use changes overall; and, in particular, designate biodiversity-critical areas for protection based on comprehensive ecological, social, and economic assessments, withdrawing them from intensive use where necessary.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, increase the benefits of nature to people through ecosystem services derived from nature-based solutions.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: On track to achieve target
reportedActions: In implementing Target 9, Mongolia has regulated biodiversity conservation and the reduction of ecosystem degradation at the legal level through environmental protection and related sectoral laws, thereby strengthening the policy and institutional foundations. In particular, the Green Development Policy, approved by the State Great Khural through Resolution №43 (2014), defined the concept of ecosystem services and proposed establishing payment and incentive mechanisms between service beneficiaries and those who contribute to maintaining services sustainably. This marked an important starting point for mainstreaming the ecosystem services approach into policy and planning. Constitutional amendments in 2019 further enshrined the right to live in a healthy and safe environment and the right to access information on environmental impacts arising from the use of subsoil resources; in line with these changes, revisions have begun to be introduced to legislation on water, forests, rangelands, and protected areas. Under the “Vision-2050” long-term policy, Mongolia set directions to improve regulatory arrangements for ecosystem service valuation, update ecological–economic valuation methodologies, and increase public awareness of their value and importance. In addition, economic instruments related to ecosystem services are being implemented through various fees and charges, including land fees, air pollution charges, hunting permits, and fees for the use of water and mineral springs, natural plants, and timber harvesting. “The Law on Natural Resource Use Fees” sets fee rates for the use of resources such as plants, water, forests, and wildlife, serving as an incentive for sustainable use. Moreover, Mongolia has begun applying updated methodologies for assessing damages to water resources and revised ecological–economic valuations for selected plant species and wildlife, representing practical improvements in valuation tools. Under policies to expand the protected area network and conserve ecosystem structure, Mongolia has worked to enlarge the network and improve management plans and protection measures. In 2015, with support from a United Nations Development Programme project, assessments of ecosystem services provided by selected protected areas were conducted, supporting initial efforts to measure “conservation benefits” through ecosystem services. Through continued expansion of the protected area network and related projects, key measures have been implemented to reduce ecosystem degradation and restore ecosystem services and nature’s benefits to people, including by integrating these actions into local planning processes. Projects such as “Ensuring the resilience and stability of Mongolia’s native ecosystems” have supported improvements to green development legislation and financing mechanisms, the integration of biodiversity and ecosystem service conservation measures into local development plans, capacity building, and valuation and mapping of ecosystem services—representing concrete steps to translate target implementation into local-level planning. In addition, Mongolia has strengthened the legal framework to regulate the use of natural resources for household, special, and industrial purposes, and to grant access based on research, monitoring, and management plans. This has increased opportunities to shift natural resource use from a “permit-only” approach toward use that is grounded in evidence and planning.

progressItems.progressSummary: The concept of ecosystem services (e.g., water provision, soil protection, climate regulation, food and raw materials, and cultural values) has begun to be integrated into policy and planning, with strengthened legal and policy foundations. The National Adaptation Plan (NAP) includes provisions to protect and restore water-related ecosystem services. Work has been undertaken to introduce methodologies for ecosystem service valuation at the level of protected areas and river basins, compile baseline information, and prepare assessment and research reports. Pilot ecosystem service valuations were carried out during 2019–2023 in Bayankhongor, Govi-Altai, Bulgan, and Khentii aimags, and were incorporated into local development plans, marking an initial step toward using valuation results in decision-making. A methodology was also developed to estimate the total value of forest ecosystem services, including the value of forest resources and non-timber forest products as well as indirect benefits-covering seven service categories: protecting forests, water, soils, and biodiversity; carbon storage; and recreation . In Mongolia, economic incentives for sustainable natural resource use and financing sources for conservation and restoration have been established through regulatory instruments such as land fees, air pollution charges, and fees for the use of water and mineral springs, forests, wildlife, and natural plant resources. “The Law on Natural Resource Use Fees” sets fee rates for the use of resources including plants, water and mineral springs, forests, and wildlife, and establishes provisions for allocating a defined share of fee revenues to environmental protection and restoration measures. Related regulations and ecological–economic valuation methodologies have also been updated and are being implemented. However, the allocation and use of fee revenues for environmental protection and restoration in line with legal and regulatory requirements has not been fully implemented, posing a constraint to sustainable financing. In 2020, the Asia Foundation conducted a study on the feasibility of calculating ecosystem service payments in “green zones,” forest and water fund areas, and their protection zones, including an assessment of international experts. Researchers from the Physical Geography Division of the Institute of Geography and Geoecology, Mongolian Academy of Sciences carried out a study on determining the ecosystem value of the Lake Khövsgöl Strictly Protected Area and calculating ecosystem service payments, developing a methodology for estimating ecosystem service values. Other domestic and international researchers have also been undertaking studies in this field. As part of piloting ecosystem service payment mechanisms, initiatives have been implemented in project target areas to protect rangeland ecosystems, reduce degradation, and support restoration through: (1) providing incentives for livestock sales to herder households that reduce herd sizes to match pasture carrying capacity; and (2) establishing a “Risk Fund” to support the implementation of five-year integrated plans of herder groups. Following pilot implementation of livestock-sale incentives with 225 herder groups, end-of-year livestock census results for 2022 showed a 23.4% reduction in total livestock numbers—10.1 percentage points higher than among non-participating herders. Building on this initiative, Bayantsagaan soum of Bayankhongor aimag continued the pilot in 2023, and as a result 614 herder households across 17 herder groups reduced their livestock by 160.2 thousand sheep units, thereby relieving grazing pressure and freeing up pasture areas . Under the SPAN project (2010–2015) implemented by the United Nations Development Programme and the Global Environment Facility (GEF), the need to assess the contribution of the protected area network to the economy was highlighted, and a network-level assessment as well as valuations for three pilot sites (including Gorkhi–Terelj National Park and Ikh Nart Nature Reserve) were conducted, demonstrating the value of ecosystem services provided by protected areas. In Tsenkher soum, Arkhangai aimag, the value of rangeland provisioning services and the benefits herders obtain from ecosystems were also estimated Under air pollution reduction policies, regulatory and enforcement measures have been implemented to improve fuel use and modernize heating devices, phase out non-compliant equipment, and strengthen compliance with standards. Nationwide, the fixed air quality monitoring network has been expanded, the capacity of automatic stations has been increased, and data flows have been improved. Projects to protect drinking water sources and upgrade water supply networks in both urban and rural areas have been implemented, alongside measures to improve access to safe drinking water. To protect urban water resources, solutions for reusing treated wastewater, including for industrial uses such as thermal power plants have been piloted, and related infrastructure upgrades are underway. Overall, Mongolia has established a foundation for maintaining and restoring nature’s contributions to people by supporting ecosystem conservation, sustainable use, and local participation.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Challenges remain, including the need to address financing, improve the frequency of baseline studies, and strengthen data and quantitative information. Going forward, combining ecosystem-based solutions with economic incentives and collaborative governance will increase the effectiveness of achieving the target.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: If Mongolia can expand the protected area network while appropriately reducing grazing pressure, restoring water sources, and effectively enforcing the legal framework for damage assessment and compensation, the foundation for achieving the target of restoring and enhancing ecosystem services will be substantially strengthened. Under the project “Ensuring the resilience and stability of Mongolia’s native ecosystems,” the values of ecosystem services in selected priority areas were assessed and mapped. Baseline information was compiled to support a development model in which aimags and soums use natural resources efficiently and sustainably, sustain ecosystem services, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and waste, ensure social participation, and contribute to poverty reduction. At the local level, this created an initial pilot model for developing organic policy solutions and alternatives—grounded in green development principles aligned with local carrying capacity—prioritizing tourism and livestock-based livelihoods while avoiding mining-based pathways. Building on the ecosystem service valuation and mapping baseline, Zavkhan Province prepared its medium-term local development planning document, the “Five-year Strategic Directions for Developing Zavkhan Aimag (2021–2025).” The national air quality monitoring network has been expanded, with automatic monitoring stations installed across all 21 aimags, enabling continuous monitoring and assessment. In Ulaanbaatar, the ban on household use of raw coal (Government Resolution No. 62 of 2018) and the introduction of improved processed fuel have produced tangible progress in reducing pollution from household fuel combustion, and a downward trend in air pollution levels has been observed.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, increase the area of urban green and blue infrastructure.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: Urban green and blue infrastructures include greeneries and blue (water bodies) elements in capital city, aimag, soum, village and settlements. Regarding aimag centers, the amount of green space per person varies; according to 2023 data, Baruun-Urt city leads with 237 square meters per capita . In contrast, Ulaanbaatar city's green space per person was 5.1 square meters in 2021 and rose to 6.5 square meters in 2023, with plans to reach 15 square meters by 2030 . In terms of total area, 2022 data shows that Ulaanbaatar's green space covers 637.7 hectares. This is a 3.6-fold increase compared to 2010 figures, while the green space per capita has increased 3.5 times over the same period . The "One Billion Trees" national movement was launched in 2021 under the initiative of the President of Mongolia, U. Khurelsukh . It is being successfully implemented, with 84 million trees planted as of 2024 , a certain percentage of which have been planted in urban green spaces. In 2024, the "Urban Building Regulations"  were developed, specifying the required amount of green space within construction sites. These regulations also include provisions for establishing "blue infrastructure," such as fountains, within public green areas. Regarding Ulaanbaatar city, there were 145 registered fountains as of 2020, of which 50 are currently operational . The Action Program for Developmnet of Mongolia 2024–2028 includes the establishment of "20-Minute Cities." Within this framework, several initiatives are planned, including the expansion of green spaces and the construction of dams and reservoirs for flood water management. To reduce flood risk in Ulaanbaatar and create surface water accumulation, an artificial lake with a capacity of 300,000 cubic meters was created in 2024 at Sanzai, the source of the Selbe River, and is now open to the public . As of 2025, the Office of the Governor of Ulaanbaatar city has developed a plan to increase green space per capita and improve the recreational environment for citizens. This plan identifies 32 potential locations covering a total of 4,920 hectares for greening and landscaping projects to be implemented between 2025 and 2030. Since 2018, four major green spaces have been established along the Tuul River .

progressItems.progressSummary: By 2030, the goal is to increase the area of urban green and blue infrastructure to 35% and raise the green space per capita to 15 sq.m. However, current performance remains insufficient. Specifically, plans to expand urban water structures aimed for 14 reservoirs and water facilities by 2024 and 38 by 2030, but implementation is currently lagging. Therefore, intensive efforts are required to immediately increase green and blue infrastructure to establish an ecological balance in urban areas. Doing so will strengthen the climate change resilience of urban ecosystems and create opportunities to support biodiversity. This target has been newly incorporated into NBSAP, and there has been measurable progress in expanding urban green spaces in the recent years. As of 2023, the green space per capita has increased 3.5-fold compared to 2010 levels. Provincial centers in the Gobi and steppe regions with lower population density currently lead in this metric (for example, Baruun-Urt at 237 sq.m and Altai at 100 sq.m per capita). However, efforts to expand blue infrastructure are proceeding slowly.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Major challenges encountered are: •    There is a lack of policy enforcement and implementation regarding green and blue infrastructure standards. For instance, until 2024, the required amount of green space in construction projects were not fully enforced or adequately met . •    Although a draft law focused on green infrastructure was developed, it has not yet been approved. The government set an objective to finalize and pass this legislation in 2021 . •    Furthermore, stakeholder participation remains weak in the areas of tree planting, as well as the maintenance and protection of green and blue infrastructure. Therefore, it is necessary to launch public awareness campaigns and actively involve the community.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: Within the framework of the "One Billion Trees" national movement, strategic plans are underway to plant 130 million trees to expand urban green spaces and 209 million trees to establish green infrastructure . By organizing spring and autumn planting events (2 times per year), the movement is successfully increasing urban greenery, fostering multistakeholder participation, and enhancing the ecological awareness of the public. A notable example of these efforts is the "One Billion Trees" Fund, initiated by the banking and financial sector . Since 2022, this fund has annually selected and supported projects to increase green space; in 2023 alone, it facilitated the creation of over 20,000 square meters of green space and the planting of 105,000 trees. In addition, to improve air and environmental quality while mitigating flood risks, Mongolia has also begun establishing reservoirs, ponds, and man-made lakes in urban areas. A key project is the 300,000 cubic meter reservoir in the Sanzai valley of Ulaanbaatar, which is currently utilized for recreation, tourism, and educational purposes .

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, develop a comprehensive database for genetic resources and traditional knowledge, while strengthening legal and governance frameworks to ensure the fair and equitable sharing of benefits.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: By acceding to the Nagoya Protocol in 2012, Mongolia established and developed a system for registering its genetic resources and traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources, enabling the fair and equitable sharing of benefits and the incorporation of these resources into economic activities, thereby creating opportunities to derive benefits from them. A legal and regulatory framework has been established to govern relations related to the registration, assessment of status, conservation, protection, research and development, utilization of genetic resources and traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources, as well as the free exchange of seeds and samples for research and educational purposes. In this regard, the State Great Khural adopted the Law on Genetic Resources in 2021. In connection with the implementation of this law, the following regulations were approved and enacted in 2022: “Regulation on the Establishment, Maintenance, Use, Storage, and Protection of the Registry and Database of Genetic Resources and Traditional Knowledge Associated with Genetic Resources”; “Regulation on the Identification of Holders of Traditional Knowledge Associated with Genetic Resources and on Obtaining Prior Informed Consent for the Use of Such Traditional Knowledge”; “Regulation on the Establishment of Gene Banks and on the Enrichment, Registration, Conservation, Distribution, and Exchange of Gene Bank Collections”. Furthermore, in 2022, in accordance with Article 12.4 of the Law on Genetic Resources, a Mongolian National Standard specifying the general requirements for the storage of specimens and samples maintained under laboratory conditions was approved. In 2017, the Law on Animal Genetic Resources was adopted and subsequently amended and improved in 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024. In 2019, the “Regulation on the structure of the National Registry and Unified Database of Animal Genetic Resources” and the “Regulation on the Establishing and Reporting the National Registry and Unified Database of Animal Genetic Resources” were approved. In 2018, the State Great Khural ratified the International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture, enabling the free exchange of seeds and samples for research and educational purposes. The revised Law on Crop Seeds and Varieties , adopted in 2021, included provisions on the conservation and sustainable use of genetic resources for food and agricultural crops.

Therefore, specialized centers for genetic resources have been established, and gene banks and registration systems for genetic resources are being developed. In this regard, gene banks of plants, animals, and microorganisms stored at Institute of Biology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences, the Botanical Garden and research institute of Mongolian Academy of Sciences, the herbarium of the National University of Mongolia, and the Natural History Museum are being expanded and strengthened. In addition, in 2022, the “Erdenet” Forest Genetic Resources Center was established with a seed storage facility of 1,000 tons capacity. The center focuses on the establishment of seed banks for rare, economically valuable, and woody plant species; the conservation and protection of forest genetic resources; the conduct of experiments and research; and the introduction of cultivated forest resources into economic circulation. As a result, seeds and propagation materials of woody plants are now stored in specialized facilities and utilized for reforestation activities. Pursuant to the Law on Animal Genetic Resources, the National Livestock Gene Bank Center was established in 2018 at the national, regional, and species levels and has been continuously strengthened. Its core functions include the conservation and protection of livestock genetic resources from degradation, extinction, and loss; the establishment of registration and information databases; the improvement of livestock quality and breed characteristics; the application, localization, and dissemination of biotechnological advances in breeding, reproduction, and related services; and the conduct of molecular and genetic analyses of breeds, strains, and their breeding products. As of 2025, the National Livestock Gene Bank Center preserves 38,000 doses of cryopreserved semen from 39 livestock breeds and strains in its gene bank. During the period 2022–2025, laparoscopic artificial insemination services were successfully provided to 30,741 cattle and 2,343 sheep. Within the framework of the implementation of the Law on Animal Genetic Resources, the status of animal genetic resources was assessed, evaluated, and reported in 2021 . Livestock registration, genetic evaluation, and herd turnover data are now obtained electronically from the Integrated Livestock Management System. In addition, general characteristics of Mongolian livestock breeds and strains have been entered and registered in the DAD-IS (Domestic Animal Diversity Information System) database.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: However, challenges remain in deriving both monetary and non-monetary benefits from Mongolia’s abundant genetic resources and traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources. In particular, Mongolia still lacks an effective system and comprehensive legal framework for the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources and traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources. Due to the absence of utilization cases involving genetic resources or traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources that have been issued an Internationally Recognized Certificate of Compliance through benefit-sharing intermediary mechanisms, the country has not been able to realize benefits from the use of its genetic resources and related traditional knowledge. Furthermore, due to a lack of qualified human resources and limited laboratory capacity continue to hinder the conduct of molecular and genetic analyses and the assessment of genetic resources of livestock breeds and strains, agricultural crops, natural plant species, and their breeding products. Going forward, it is necessary to ensure that samples and specimens in the genetic resources fund are stored in accordance with international standards; to conduct detailed inventories of the preserved samples and specimens; to link the national electronic registry on the utilization of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge with the ABS Clearing-House (ABSCH) database; to establish a legal framework regulating benefit-sharing payments arising from the utilization of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge; to obtain an Internationally Recognized Certificate of Compliance (IRCC); and thereby enable holders of genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge to begin receiving both monetary and non-monetary benefits.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030,  Integrate biodiversity issues into the policies and planning of all sectors.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: On track to achieve target
reportedActions: M ongolia is implementing the following key measures to integrate biodiversity (BD) into cross-sectoral policies and planning: • The National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) (2015–2025) has been approved and is under implementation, serving as the core policy document for aligning biodiversity conservation with national development policies. • Initial steps have been taken to integrate biodiversity conservation into the policies of sectors beyond the environment sector, including agriculture, livestock, and forestry, where natural resource use is dominant. • The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA ) has been piloted since 2018 with the support of UNESCAP, creating an initial foundation for using quantitative natural resource data in policy and decision-making. In this context, the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, the Ministry of Mining and Heavy Industry, and the Agency for Land Administration, Geodesy and Cartography have been conducting partial natural resource accounts. • The Law on Fees for the Use of Natural Resources explicitly defines funding sources for environmental protection, thereby establishing a legal framework to improve the linkage between resource use and conservation. • Mongolia’s accession as an associate member to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) has enhanced opportunities to collect, use, and apply national biodiversity data in policy formulation in accordance with international standards. • The National “One Health” Strategy was approved in 2022, reflecting the interlinkages between environmental, human, and animal health at the policy level, representing a significant advancement in jointly addressing biodiversity loss, climate change, and zoonotic disease risks. • Research conducted by the Mongolian Academy of Sciences (2021–2024) identified that water scarcity in the Gobi and desert regions, degradation of green zones, and wildlife migration constitute underlying risk factors for the transmission of infectious diseases, providing important scientific evidence for evidence-based policymaking. • The adoption of the Law on Development Policy, Planning and Its Management (2020) established a legal framework for ensuring coherence and an integrated monitoring and evaluation system across long-, medium-, and short-term national development policies. • The long-term development policy “ Vision–2050 ” has been adopted, positioning sustainable development and environmental protection as fundamental principles of national development. • Cross-sectoral coordination bodies have been established, including the National Committee on Sustainable Development, the National Climate Committee, and the National Committee on Reducing Air Pollution. However, the roles and responsibilities of sectors, as well as monitoring, evaluation, and financing mechanisms , remain insufficiently defined.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, establish systems to monitor and transparently report the impacts, risks, and outcomes of business activities regarding biodiversity.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: On track to achieve target
reportedActions: In Mongolia, the following foundational measures have begun to be implemented to ensure transparent disclosure of the impacts and risks of business activities on biodiversity (BD): Companies listed on the Mongolian Stock Exchange have gradually begun to disclose environmental information to the public and to conduct sustainability impact assessments. Regulations on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) reporting have been partially introduced since 2022, with large enterprises voluntarily preparing ESG reports. Within the framework of the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD), the Bank of Mongolia and relevant institutions have initiated efforts to develop legal frameworks and methodologies to integrate nature- and climate-related risks into financial decision-making. The long-term development policy “Vision–2050” has identified Green Development as a priority in fiscal and development policy, serving as a foundational policy to promote environmentally friendly businesses and sustainable production. In 2025, a readiness assessment for the implementation of sustainability disclosure standards in Mongolia was conducted, covering 189 organizations across the mining, finance, manufacturing, and service sectors. For the first time, the assessment comprehensively evaluated the current state of businesses’ environmental practices, natural resource use, risk management, and transparency in reporting. The report shows that while companies collect environmental information to a certain extent, a systematic framework for reporting impacts, dependencies, and risks related to biodiversity has not yet been fully developed. With the participation of the Ministry of Finance and relevant institutions, policy discussions and pilot initiatives have begun to gradually introduce sustainability disclosures under IFRS S1 and S2. This is laying the groundwork for embedding risk-based reporting concepts within the business sector . The Biodiversity Finance Initiative (BIOFIN) is being implemented in Mongolia, supporting the identification of biodiversity financing needs and opportunities, as well as capacity-building activities. The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, in cooperation with international organizations, has begun implementing incentives and reward mechanisms to promote green businesses (e.g., Green Awards and initiatives under the BIOFIN framework).

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, minimize overconsumption and waste through supporting public education on sustainable consumption.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: Mongolia has laid the foundation for behavioral change to reduce overconsumption and waste through integrated measures at the policy, education, infrastructure, and community levels. Key actions include strengthening the legal framework on waste management, introducing waste sorting systems, promoting public participation, and integrating sustainable consumption education into formal curricula. Pursuant to Order No. A/404 (1 August 2025) of the Minister of Education, the revised Preschool Education Curriculum was approved, incorporating content on water and energy conservation, waste separation, recycling, and responsible resource use. Additionally, the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, initiated the integration of climate change content into the national curriculum for grades 1–12 . Within the framework of implementing the objectives and measures outlined in key policy documents such as “Vision–2050” (2020), the “National Program on Education for Sustainable Development (2018–2022)”, and the “National Program for Improving Waste Management (2012–2022)”, strategically important projects have been successfully implemented at both national and municipal levels with the support of international partners. Strategic projects supported by international partners have further reinforced implementation. These include: Phase II of the Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) project (2019–2022); The wastewater recycling plant under the Second Compact Agreement with the United States Millennium Challenge Corporation ; The “9202-MON: Ulaanbaatar Community Food Waste Recycling” project implemented with the Asian Development Bank; The “Switching On the Green Economy (SOGE)” project under the EU SWITCH-Asia Programme; The implementation and ongoing revision of the Regulation on Incentivizing Organizations that Introduce Environmentally Friendly Advanced Technologies (Government Resolution No. 290 of 2017), which operationalizes the “Green Certificate” and “Eco Label” mechanisms The Regulation is currently under comprehensive review and revision to strengthen its policy coherence, improve its implementation mechanisms, and enhance its overall effectiveness and impact in advancing sustainable production and consumption. The “Ulaanbaatar Solid Waste Modernisation Project,” financed by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) with a grant from the European Union.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, enhance the legislative, governance, and monitoring systems for genetically modified organisms.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: On track to achieve target
reportedActions: Mongolia acceded to the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety to the Convention on Biological Diversity in 2002, and in 2012 joined the Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur Supplementary Protocol on Liability and Redress , actively ensuring their implementation. In particular, in 2007, Mongolia adopted the Law on Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs) to regulate all types of activities related to GMOs developed through modern biotechnology in a manner that poses no risk to human health or the environment. Additionally, provisions were included in the Law on Food to register and publicly disclose foods derived from GMOs, and to prohibit the import of GMO-derived foods through foreign loans or aid. Mongolia has implemented procedures for risk assessment and registration of raw materials and products derived from GMOs , and has established and introduced 6 sets of laboratory MNS standards for detecting GMO-derived products in food. In 2025, under the regional project “Promoting the safe application of biotechnology through Multi-country Cooperation in the implementation of National Biosafety Frameworks in Asia”, Mongolia reported an Inventory report on Biotechnology and Biosafety in Mongolia [1] . progressItems.progressSummary: In order to implement this national target, one of the key measures undertaken by Mongolia has been the establishment of a legal and regulatory framework governing relations related to the development, use, transboundary movement, and biosafety of GMOs within the territory of the country. In particular, within the framework of the implementation of the Law on Food, Mongolia has ceased the acceptance of GMO-derived food products through foreign loans and assistance in order to ensure biosafety. Mongolia has established validated methodologies to detect GMOs and derived products in food at both protein and nucleic acid levels by applying Mongolian National Standards (MNS), including Foodstuffs — Methods for the detection of GMOs and derived products — General requirements and definitions; Foodstuffs — Methods for the detection of GMOs and derived products — Nucleic acid-based methods; Foodstuffs — GMOs and derived products — Quantitative nucleic acid-based methods; and Foodstuffs — Methods for the detection of GMOs and derived products — Protein-based methods. Furthermore, the current status of human resources and technical capacity of biotechnology and biosafety laboratories in universities and research institutions has been comprehensively assessed.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Although Mongolia regulates activities related to the development, use, transboundary movement, and biosafety of GMOs through laws, regulations, and standards, challenges remain. The National Biosafety Clearing-House (BCH) platform, intended to facilitate information exchange, transparency, and decision-making among Parties to the Cartagena Protocol, is not yet fully operational. The procedures for Advance Informed Agreement (AIA) have not been consistently applied in practice. Risk assessments for cultivated GMOs, the public disclosure of reports, and measures to prevent potential risks arising from GMOs are insufficient. progressItems.targetText: By 2030, reform subsidies and incentives that have negative impacts on biodiversity, while increasing environmentally positive (green) incentives.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: Progress towards target but at an insufficient rate
reportedActions: In alignment with Target 18 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), Mongolia has initiated evidence-based analytical work to identify, assess, and redesign subsidies and incentives that may have negative impacts on biodiversity [1]. In this context, a comprehensive analysis was conducted under UNDP BIOFIN Phase II, covering subsidies, incentives, tax exemptions, and tax relief measures implemented in the agriculture, energy, and transport sectors, and assessing their direct and indirect impacts on biodiversity. Capacity-building and awareness-raising training sessions on subsidy reform were organized for policy makers, civil servants, and relevant stakeholders, introducing the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) / BIOFIN methodology, impact assessment approaches, international good practices, and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) requirements. Based on the findings of the analysis, policy options for redesigning milk and wheat subsidies were developed, together with impact assessments, feasible implementation pathways, and action plans to support evidence-based decision-making. At present, Mongolia is assessed to have made measurable progress in the identification, prioritization, and development of policy options for subsidies and incentives that are harmful to biodiversity. At the sectoral level—notably in agriculture, energy, and transport—inventories of existing subsidies have been compiled and initial impact assessments have been conducted, enabling the identification of priority harmful subsidies. However, as policy decisions to abolish, reduce, or fully redirect these subsidies toward biodiversity-positive (green) incentives have not yet been implemented, progress toward achieving the target is assessed as moderate. progressItems.progressSummary: Key Results and Current Status A study on subsidies potentially harmful to biodiversity identified the main economic sectors—mining, livestock, agriculture, transport, services, light industry, and construction—that face difficulties in reducing negative impacts. These sectors’ limited positive contributions to biodiversity exacerbate environmental degradation and increase conservation costs. From 2014–2023, Mongolia provided MNT 7.1 trillion in government subsidies, of which MNT 1.0 trillion (14%) were considered harmful or potentially harmful to biodiversity. This accounts for 0.8% of total government spending and shows an increasing trend. Sector-specific breakdowns: Agriculture: MNT 40 billion (direct subsidies) Energy losses: MNT 276 billion Transport support: MNT 350 billion Increased water use: MNT 9 billion Private sector support (unspecified): MNT 315 billion [1] Out of 50 types of subsidies identified as harmful: 29 are harmful (24 in agriculture), 21 are potentially harmful (16 in agriculture) [2] . The portfolio budget of the Minister of Environment and Climate change (MNT 0.9 trillion) is lower than the estimated volume of biodiversity-harmful subsidies (MNT 1.0 trillion), indicating a clear policy inconsistency. An integrated registry and system for environmentally friendly (green-criteria) subsidies and incentives, along with a proper MRV (monitoring–reporting–verification) framework, remain insufficient. [1] BIOFIN. (2024). Study on Biodiversity-Harmful Subsidies. [2] BIOFIN. (2024). Study on Biodiversity-Harmful Subsidies. p. 20.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Key Challenges The main challenges are that subsidy policies are sensitive socio-economic issues, which slows political decision-making, coordination between sectors is weak, and there is a lack of a consistent monitoring system to measure the actual impacts of subsidies. Harmful subsidies have been identified but not yet translated into policy decisions. Systematic assessments of social and economic impacts have not been conducted. There are few practical examples or mechanisms for green incentives. In the agriculture sector, the MRV system is weak, and policies linking it to the carbon market are not fully developed. Possible Ways Forward Ensure cross-sectoral coordination in the planning of subsidy and incentive policies. Introduce environmental impact monitoring and evaluation of subsidies and incentives. Redesign potentially harmful subsidies and incentives in the agriculture, energy, and transport sectors. Revise and update up to five policies or regulations related to biodiversity-harmful subsidies and incentives by introducing green criteria.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: Under the BIOFIN II project, alternative models for redesigning dairy subsidies were developed, taking into account the potential to reduce pasture degradation and greenhouse gas emissions caused by livestock population growth, while transitioning to productivity- and quality-based incentives. This serves as a practical example, demonstrating that such a model can reduce negative environmental impacts while maintaining sustainable income for herders. Transparent information on subsidies in the public transport, energy, and agriculture sectors, along with audit findings and policy review studies (e.g., Think Mongol’s policy review), have communicated issues of subsidy data, transparency, and impacts to the public in an understandable way, contributing to the creation of an enabling environment for policy reform.

progressItems.targetText: Substantially and progressively increase financial resources towards biodiversity conservation from all sources, in an effective, timely, innovative and easily accessible manner.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: On track to achieve target
reportedActions: T rends in State Budget Financing Between 2020 and 2024, environmental expenditure declined from MNT 210–229 billion to MNT 121–112 billion in 2022–2023 but increased again to MNT 216 billion in 2024. Use of Natural Resource Use Fees (NRUF) The implementation rate of the legal requirement to reinvest NRUF revenues back into environmental protection declined from 44.7% in 2017 to 26% in 2021 but improved to 62.6% in 2023 and 64.3% in 2024 because of the BIOFIN project and related policy measures. The implementation rate of the legal requirement to reinvest NRUF revenues back into environmental protection declined from 44.7% in 2017 to 26% in 2021 but improved to 62.6% [2] in 2023 and 64.3% in 2024 because of the MECC, BIOFIN project and related policy measures that strengthened enforcement, regulation revisions, transparency, and local budgeting capacity. In 2024, total revenue reached MNT 284.0 billion, with a spending threshold set at MNT 77.6 billion and an approved budget of MNT 77.4 billion. Of this, MNT 47.4 billion was allocated to environmental expenditure. The overall implementation rate stood at 64.3%, contributing to significant biodiversity outcomes, including the implementation of over 4,200 conservation and rehabilitation measures nationwide between 2022 and 2024. Private Sector Engagement Private sector environmental expenditure was around MNT 1 billion in 2020–2021, doubled from 2022 onwards, and stabilized at MNT 2.7–2.8 billion during 2023–2024. Green Finance As of Q4 2024, the outstanding balance of “green loans” issued by Mongolian commercial banks reached MNT 1.3 trillion, accounting for 3.7% of total loans. Reform Toward Results-Based Financing The Government has set a goal to shift budgetary and external financing toward results-based financing, with implementation initiated in the education and health sectors. New Financial Mechanisms In April 2024, the “Mongolia’s Natural Heritage” Conservation Trust Fund, based on diversified funding sources, was established . Using the updated BIOFIN methodology and results-based costing (RBC), the total financing need for implementing the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) in Mongolia for 2026–2030 was estimated at 2.8 trillion MNT. This indicates that an average annual investment equivalent to 0.5–0.7% of GDP will be required. In terms of financing structure, 88% of the costs are investment-type expenditures, and by source, 70% is expected from the private sector, with the remainder covered by national and local budgets and international funding. This highlights the need for a practical strategy to mobilize financing from multiple sources.

progressItems.progressSummary: Key Results In 2024, MNT 216 billion was allocated from the state budget for environmental protection and restoration. Total environmental expenditure increased from MNT 560 billion in 2015 to MNT 865 billion in 2024, representing a 55% increase. Of the MNT 197.4 billion required to implement the National Biodiversity Programme (2016–2025), 69.2% remains without clearly identified funding sources.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Key Challenges The share of environmental expenditure in GDP (0.43%) is low compared to countries with similar mining-based economies. Environmental financing data are fragmented across multiple systems with weak interoperability. Results-based budgeting, monitoring, and evaluation systems are not yet fully developed. There is a shortage of specialized human resources in environmental finance and economic policy. Possible Ways Forward Strengthen financing mechanisms for conservation activities and increase private sector investment within environmental and social responsibility frameworks. Gradually increase the share of environmental sector expenditure in GDP to align with international benchmarks. Adopt the revised Law on Natural Resource Use Fees and strengthen its implementation. Transition total environmental sector financing to a results-based budgeting framework. Modernize and integrate databases on environmental protection and restoration expenditures by linking them with other government information systems. Establish a legal framework to collect the “Natural Heritage Fee” from foreign visitors and allocate it to conservation activities. Improve the legal framework for biodiversity offset mechanisms to increase conservation-related revenues. Explore and pilot biodiversity credits and other innovative financing mechanisms for conservation.
progressItems.actionEffectivenessSummary: As a result of the BIOFIN project, spending of NRUF revenues increased and environmental financing improved. A 2022 Government Resolution enabled the digitalization of reporting on environmental fee expenditures, creating conditions for regular monitoring. The targets for 2016–2018 and 2022–2025 can be considered largely achieved based on available evidence. However, for the 2019–2021 period, concrete and measurable evaluation data are limited, indicating the need for more detailed research based on additional sources. In the environment and climate sectors, 28 projects and programs are currently being implemented with total funding of USD 182.4 million. According to data from the Environmental Information Database , between 1998 and 2023, 107 projects and programs have been approved and implemented, with approximately USD 360 million spent . Source: MECC Of this, one-third of the total financing has been allocated to projects and programs implemented in protected areas. Approximately 24% has been spent on climate change initiatives. The reason for the higher funding in protected areas is that international biodiversity-focused donor organizations prefer to finance measures that provide long-term sustainable benefits, such as protected areas and conservation activities. As of 2024, 28 projects are being implemented with funding from international organizations including the Global Environment Facility, South Korea, Germany, the Green Climate Fund, the European Union, Japan, and the Asian Development Bank. In terms of financing and investment: “Eternal Mongolia” Program: The Government of Mongolia provided USD 127 million and international donors USD 71 million to co-finance a 15-year project under the “Project Finance for Permanence” model to expand conservation and the national protected area network BIOFIN Phase II (UNDP’s Biodiversity Finance Initiative) : Implemented from 2019 to 2030 to bridge the biodiversity finance gap. To date, a total of USD 71,002,466 has been invested, with the project starting at USD 4.85 million in 2019 and continuing at USD 6.15 million in 2024. Natural Resource Use Fees (NRUF): Revenues allocated to conservation reached USD 11.9 million in 2023, a 170% increase compared to the 2016–2021 average, with further increases expected in 2024. Green Climate Fund Financing: Between 2021 and 2025, projects and programs totaling USD 436 million were approved, of which USD 70 million is allocated for restoration and USD 23 million for climate adaptation measures. “Green Loan” interest subsidy: In 2024, 1.5 billion MNT has been allocated in the budget for interest subsidies. Discounted loans are being provided to individuals and businesses for energy-saving and environmentally friendly products.

progressItems.targetText: Strengthen capacity-building and development, access to and transfer of technology, and promote development of and access to innovation and technical and scientific cooperation in biodiversity conservation.
progressItems.levelOfProgress: No significant change
reportedActions: T o promote innovation and scientific and technical cooperation in the field of biodiversity conservation, activities are being implemented within the framework of the following laws: the Law on Science and Technology (2024), the Law on Innovation (2012) , the Law on Technology Transfer (1998), and the Law on Patents (2021). The Medium-Term Sustainable Development Policy of Mongolia and the Government’s Action Program include the priority objective of “Developing the Science, Technology, and Innovation Sector” and outline plans for its implementation. In addition, Section 2.4 of Mongolia’s long-term development policy “Vision 2050” sets the goal of “Developing a nationally competitive science, technology, and innovation system,” which is planned and being implemented in three phases. The Government of Mongolia’s “ Priority Directions for Innovation Activities (2020–2025)” outlines objectives to support Made in Mongolia innovations, develop artificial intelligence, big data, digital, and emerging technologies, and strengthen the capacity to produce national innovative products through public-private collaboration. Since 2022, the Science and Technology Fund (STF) has been organizing the campaign “Promoting Science, Technology, and Innovation in the Regions across all 12 provinces. In 2022, the “Erdenet” Science and Technology Park was established to conduct scientific and technological research, provide training, and carry out production and innovation activities, with the aim of transforming the traditionally mining-dominated economic structure into a digital economy based on high technology, knowledge, and innovation. In 2022, 17.2% of the Science and Technology sector ’s expenditures were allocated to natural sciences, and 4.1% to agricultural and veterinary sciences. The budget for the Science and Technology sector increased from MNT 43 billion in 2020 to MNT 105.8 billion in 2024. However, this still represents only 0.14% of GDP. Figure. Structure and share of expenditures in the Science and Technology sector In 2025, the Science and Technology Fund (STF) plans to launch 32 new projects, while 112 ongoing projects will continue. Specifically, these include 24 fundamental projects, 15 commissioned projects, 1 core technology project, 8 technology testing and adaptation projects, and 64 international collaborative projects (of which 3 are with Taiwan, 16 with Russia, 32 with China, and 13 with Belarus). According to the STF report, a total of 2,086 projects were implemented during 2020–2025, with expenditures amounting to MNT 57.8 billion. The Ministry of Education and Science, in collaboration with the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), launched the project “Science, Technology, and Innovation Park Aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals: Strengthening Mongolia’s Policy Environment and Practical Capacity” to be implemented during 2023–2026. The Ministry of Digital Development, Innovation, and Communications has initiated efforts to strengthen the innovation ecosystem and, at its meeting on May 7, 2025, the Government approved the revised “Regulation on Financing Innovation Projects from the State Budget and Grant Allocation for Innovation Activities”. Within the framework of this objective, several major projects and programs aimed at promoting environmental innovation and technical cooperation have been successfully implemented through joint funding from the government, private sector, and international organizations. In 2024–2025, total funding in Mongolia related to the environment, climate, and sustainable development is increasing. The “Eternal Mongolia” program, implemented jointly by the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, The Nature Conservancy, and the Mongolian Heritage Fund, aims to expand Mongolia’s network of protected areas and conserve biodiversity. It represents a long-term partnership based on collaboration between the Government of Mongolia and international partners. Under this program , approximately USD 198 million in new investments is planned over 15 years to support conservation and local sustainable development in protected areas and their surrounding zones. This includes the establishment of 71 million USD “transition fund” sourced from the private sector and international donors, aimed at both accelerating conservation and local development objectives and creating a long-term sustainable financing mechanism for protected areas. This partnership contributes to biodiversity conservation, the sustainability of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems, and ultimately ensures that the people of Mongolia benefit sustainably from natural resources. A joint financing of USD 175 million by the Asian Development Bank and the Green Climate Fund (GCF) for Mongolia, targeting pasture management, climate adaptation, and sustainable rural development, has been approved. This funding plays a key role in expanding climate-related activities in Mongolia and enhancing opportunities for private sector and international financing [11] . As of 2024, 28 projects and programs in the environment and climate sector are being implemented with international funding from organizations such as the Global Environment Facility, the Green Climate Fund, the European Union, the Asian Development Bank, and others, covering a total of USD 182.4 million. According to the Environmental Information Database , a total of 107 projects and programs implemented or ongoing between 1998 and 2023 have received approximately USD 360 million in investments in this sector [12] .

progressItems.progressSummary: Under the leadership of the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change (MECC), support was provided for the development, ratification, and commencement of the National Program on Education for Sustainable Development. Mongolia has become one of the pioneering countries to establish a policy and operational framework for integrating ESD at the primary and secondary education levels. Another critical objective was the full integration of ESD into the school system and the creation of an institutional environment for green and sustainable development. Within the framework of the ESD project, the curricula of all 628 general education schools (Grades 1–12) in Mongolia were revised to include ESD content. This evolved into a nationwide movement, reaching a total of 468,000 students and 25,000 teachers. By expanding the "Eco-School" network, 2,680 teachers were trained as ESD trainers, thereby building the human resource capacity necessary to implement the program. The "Eco-School" program, which aims to localize ESD at the school and community levels, has successfully expanded. Since Mongolia joined the international "Eco-Schools" initiative in 2018, approximately 40% of all general education schools nationwide have achieved Eco-School status as of 2021.
progressItems.keyChallengesSummary: Since 2022, ESD has been integrated into the school management and operations of 32 model general education schools. Public awareness and engagement regarding ESD are expanding significantly, as evidenced by major events and statistics. In 2021, the national virtual forum "Collective Initiative and Partnership for ESD" drew 108,766 online participants—an unprecedented level of engagement for any educational event in Mongolia. In collaboration with the Ministry of Education, climate change education has been formally introduced into the general education curriculum. Within this framework, lessons on climate change have been presented to 330,000 students and 15,000 teachers across 440 schools. Furthermore, to prepare faculty for teaching these subjects at the tertiary level, a "Trainer-of-Trainers" program for the "Climate Change and Adaptation" curriculum was organized at the National University of Mongolia (NUM), involving 40 professors from six universities. This course is now a mandatory component of the university curriculum. Additionally, the following challenges and constraints can be highlighted: Frequent changes to educational curricula, syllabi, textbooks, and learning assessment regulations are undermining the operational stability of schools and teachers, thereby reducing the effectiveness of classroom instruction. The lack of a reliable and stable textbook supply chain remains an issue. This has hindered continuous quality improvement and compromised the principles of investment efficiency, leaving textbook availability challenges not fully resolved. While information accessibility and transparency are improving, there is a need to enhance data quality, coordination, and utilization. Furthermore, the capacity for data collection and verification at the local level remains inconsistent.

reportedActions: Mongolia adopted the Law on the Promotion of Gender Equality in 2011, establishing a comprehensive legal framework to ensure gender equality across political, legal, economic, social, cultural, and family relations. In support of the implementation of this law and related state policies, Mongolia has successfully implemented two national gender programmes and one strategic plan, as well as sector-specific gender programmes across 12 sectors, the capital city, 21 aimags, and 9 districts of Ulaanbaatar . The approval of the "Sectoral Strategic Plan for Ensuring Gender Equality" (2022–2031) has established conditions under which cross-sectoral coordination and collaboration are of critical importance for strengthening practical experience in implementing ratified laws, policies, and programs with gender sensitivity and assessing their impact within the framework of gender equality principles. It aims to evaluate policy implementation and implement special measures. Mongolia’s national gender equality institutional framework has been progressively strengthened through inclusive governance arrangements involving state institutions, civil society organizations, researchers, media, employees’ and employers’ representatives. This framework includes the National Committee on Gender Equality, sectoral gender councils within central government bodies, local gender councils within subnational administrations, national gender expert groups, and academic network. Their coordinated functioning is supported by the sustained and active operations of the Committee’s Secretariat, alongside the continued engagement and contributions of civil society, the private sector, and employers. The Government of Mongolia has made significant progress in mainstreaming gender across all sectors, including the environmental sector. Key legislative and strategic frameworks have been adopted to advance gender equality, such as the Law on Gender Equality (2011), the Green Development Policy (2014–2030), and Mongolia’s long-term Sustainable Development Vision 2016–2030. One of the activities and efforts undertaken by the Government of Mongolia to ensure gender equality in the environmental sector is the development and approval of the Environmental Sector Gender Strategy (2014–2030) by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism in 2014. Mongolia has demonstrated consistent engagement in gender-responsive climate/environmental policy. In 2018, the country hosted the international workshop “Sustainable Development: Gender and Development,” which produced the Ulaanbaatar Declaration for a Sustainable Future. Further advancing this agenda, Mongolia organized the “World Women’s Conference for a Green Future” in 2024. Building upon these initiatives, the “Gender Equality and Climate Change” International Conference was convened in Ulaanbaatar on 22–23 May 2025.
